renal-ch27:loop.e: The TAL (NKCC2) is the diluting segment.

renal-ch27:loop.q: The lumen-positive potential in the TAL drives paracellular reabsorption of:
renal-ch27:loop.e: K⁺ back-leak through ROMK makes the lumen ~+8 mV, pushing cations between cells.

renal-ch27:loop.q: Principal cells of the late distal tubule and collecting duct:
renal-ch27:loop.e: ENaC and ROMK under aldosterone control; water permeability needs ADH.

renal-ch27:loop.q: The early distal tubule NaCl co-transporter is blocked by:
A 70-year-old woman on long-term high-dose furosemide has muscle cramps and Mg²⁺ of 1.2 mg/dL. Her diet and bowel habits are normal. What is the main mechanism of her hypomagnesemia?
o: Loss of lumen-positive potential in the TAL
Inhibition of TRPM6 in the distal tubule
Decreased Mg²⁺ absorption in the gut
renal-ch27:loop.e: Most filtered Mg²⁺ is reabsorbed paracellularly in the TAL, driven by the lumen-positive potential that depends on NKCC2 and K⁺ recycling; loop diuretics abolish it. TRPM6 in the DCT handles only a small fraction.

renal-ch27:distal.q: Aldosterone acts on principal cells to:
o: Increase Na⁺ reabsorption and K⁺ secretion
Decrease ENaC and increase Na⁺ excretion

renal-ch27:distal.q: The medullary collecting duct is permeable to urea:

A 39-year-old man with HIV is treated with high-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for Pneumocystis pneumonia. On day 5, serum K⁺ is 6.1 mEq/L with normal aldosterone levels. Trimethoprim raises K⁺ by blocking which structure?
o: NCC in the distal convoluted tubule
NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb
renal-ch27:distal.e: Trimethoprim acts like amiloride, blocking ENaC in principal cells; this reduces the lumen-negative potential that drives K⁺ secretion through ROMK. Blocking NKCC2 would cause hypokalemia.

renal-ch27:segments.q: Which nephron segment reabsorbs most of the filtered Na⁺, glucose, amino acids, and HCO₃⁻?
renal-ch27:segments.e: The early PCT is the 'workhorse': ~65–80% of Na⁺ and water and nearly all glucose and amino acids.

renal-ch27:segments.q: Which segment is impermeable to water and is the 'diluting segment' that builds medullary hypertonicity?
o: Inner medullary collecting duct with ADH
renal-ch27:segments.e: The TAL reabsorbs Na⁺/K⁺/2Cl⁻ without water, so tubular fluid becomes dilute.

renal-ch27:segments.q: Principal cells of the collecting duct reabsorb Na⁺ through:
renal-ch27:segments.e: Aldosterone ↑ ENaC and Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase in principal cells, also ↑ K⁺ secretion. ADH inserts AQP2.

renal-ch27:segments.q: A 9-year-old boy has recurrent kidney stones, and his urine microscopy shows hexagonal crystals. Urine amino acid analysis shows excess cystine, ornithine, lysine and arginine. The defective transporter is located in which segment?
renal-ch27:segments.e: Cystinuria is a defect of the dibasic amino acid transporter in the PCT, where nearly all filtered amino acids are reabsorbed. The distal segments reabsorb almost no amino acids.

renal-ch27:regulation.q: PTH acts on the kidney to:
o: Insert AQP2 into collecting duct cells
↑ phosphate and Ca²⁺ reabsorption in the PCT
renal-ch27:regulation.e: PTH: ↑ Ca²⁺ (DCT), ↓ PO₄³⁻ (blocks NaPi in PCT), ↑ 1α-hydroxylase.

renal-ch27:regulation.q: ADH increases water reabsorption by binding which receptor on principal cells?
renal-ch27:regulation.e: V2 → cAMP → AQP2 insertion in the collecting duct. V1 mediates vasoconstriction.

renal-ch27:regulation.q: ANP released from atrial stretch causes:
o: Efferent dilation, afferent constriction, ↓ GFR and Na⁺ retention
renal-ch27:regulation.e: ANP/BNP: afferent dilation, efferent constriction and ↓ Na⁺ reabsorption → ↑ GFR and natriuresis; 'aldosterone escape' in primary hyperaldosteronism.

renal-ch27:regulation.q: A 53-year-old woman with kidney stones has serum Ca²⁺ 11.8 mg/dL, phosphate 2.1 mg/dL and an elevated PTH. Which renal action of PTH best explains her low phosphate?
o: Increased phosphate filtration from a higher GFR
Active phosphate secretion by the collecting duct
Stimulation of phosphate uptake into the bone matrix
Inhibition of Na⁺–phosphate cotransport in the PCT
renal-ch27:regulation.e: PTH reduces NaPi-IIa cotransporters in the PCT, causing phosphaturia and hypophosphatemia, while it increases Ca²⁺ reabsorption in the DCT. The collecting duct does not secrete phosphate.

renal-ch27:clearance.q: The renal clearance of substance X is greater than GFR. This means X is:
renal-ch27:clearance.e: Cx > GFR → secretion; Cx < GFR → reabsorption; Cx = GFR → filtered only.

renal-ch27:clearance.q: Ux = 100 mg/mL, V = 1 mL/min, Px = 2 mg/mL. Clearance of X is:
Clearance of a substance that is filtered and completely reabsorbed is:
renal-ch27:clearance.e: Glucose at normal plasma level has clearance ~0.

renal-ch27:clearance.q: Clearance of inulin is 125 mL/min and of urea 70 mL/min. This indicates urea is:
renal-ch27:clearance.e: Clearance below GFR means net reabsorption.

renal-ch27:clearance.q: Effective renal plasma flow is estimated using the clearance of:
renal-ch27:clearance.e: PAH is filtered and secreted almost completely in one pass; it slightly underestimates true RPF.

renal-ch27:clearance.q: ERPF = 600 mL/min and hematocrit = 40%. Renal blood flow is about:
PAH clearance underestimates true renal plasma flow by about:
In a 40-year-old man, urine inulin is 25 mg/mL, plasma inulin 0.2 mg/mL, urine PAH 12.5 mg/mL, plasma PAH 0.02 mg/mL, and urine flow 1 mL/min. What is his filtration fraction?
renal-ch27:clearance.e: GFR = (25 × 1) ÷ 0.2 = 125 mL/min and ERPF = (12.5 × 1) ÷ 0.02 = 625 mL/min, so FF = 125 ÷ 625 = 0.20. Mixing up the PAH values gives the wrong ratios.

renal-ch28:dilute.q: Without ADH, urine osmolarity can fall to about:
renal-ch28:dilute.e: Distal segments keep reabsorbing solute but not water.

renal-ch28:dilute.q: Tubular fluid at the end of the ascending limb is about:

A 34-year-old woman with schizophrenia drinks about 12 L of water a day. Her Na⁺ is 129 mEq/L and urine osmolality 55 mOsm/kg. Her ability to make such dilute urine depends mainly on NaCl reabsorption without water in which segment?
renal-ch28:dilute.e: The thick ascending limb (with the early distal tubule) reabsorbs NaCl while being impermeable to water, so it is the diluting segment; without ADH the collecting duct stays impermeable. The thin descending limb is permeable to water.

renal-ch28:concreq.q: The two requirements for forming concentrated urine are:
o: Low ADH and a hyperosmotic medullary interstitium
High ADH and a hyperosmotic medullary interstitium
High ADH and an iso-osmotic medullary interstitium
High GFR and high plasma aldosterone

renal-ch28:concreq.q: Urine specific gravity rises by 0.001 for every increase in osmolarity of about:

o: Seawater is hypotonic, causing water intoxication
It acts mainly by causing osmotic diarrhea
It blocks ADH release from the posterior pituitary
Its salt load exceeds maximal urine concentration
renal-ch28:concreq.e: Its salt load (~1200 mOsm/L) exceeds what the kidney can concentrate; extra water must be excreted to remove the salt.

renal-ch28:concreq.q: A 24-year-old man with sickle cell trait has nocturia. After overnight water deprivation, his urine osmolality reaches only 450 mOsm/kg, while ADH levels and the response to desmopressin are normal. Which requirement for concentrating urine has been lost?
renal-ch28:concreq.e: Sickling in the hypoxic, hypertonic vasa recta damages them and dissipates the medullary osmotic gradient, so water cannot be drawn out even with normal ADH (hyposthenuria). Normal ADH levels and a normal desmopressin response rule out the ADH and V2 options.

renal-ch28:countercurrent.q: The thick ascending limb can establish a gradient of about how much between lumen and interstitium?
renal-ch28:countercurrent.e: The single effect is ~200 mOsm/L; flow multiplies it to 1200–1400 at the papilla.

renal-ch28:countercurrent.q: Urea contributes to medullary hyperosmolality mainly through:
o: Active urea transport by TAL cells
Active urea secretion into the PCT
renal-ch28:countercurrent.e: Urea is passively reabsorbed from inner medullary collecting ducts via UT-A1/A3; ADH increases urea permeability there.

renal-ch28:countercurrent.q: The vasa recta preserve the medullary gradient because they:
o: Act as countercurrent exchangers with low flow
Carry about half of total renal blood flow to the medulla
Are impermeable to water and solutes
Actively pump NaCl into the interstitium
renal-ch28:countercurrent.e: Hairpin loops and sluggish flow minimize washout of solute.

renal-ch28:countercurrent.q: A low-protein diet reduces maximal urine concentrating ability because:
o: NaCl transport in the TAL is blocked
Less urea is available to the medulla
GFR rises and washes out the medulla
ADH secretion falls with less protein
renal-ch28:countercurrent.e: Less urea is available for the medullary interstitium; urea supplies 40–50% of inner medullary osmolality.

renal-ch28:countercurrent.q: A 70-year-old man on high-dose furosemide undergoes water deprivation for another reason. His urine osmolality stays near 300 mOsm/kg despite high plasma ADH. What best explains his inability to concentrate urine?
o: Blocked TAL NaCl transport abolishes the medullary gradient
Blocked ADH release from the posterior pituitary gland
Blocked urea transport in inner medullary ducts
Blocked aquaporin-2 insertion in the collecting duct
renal-ch28:countercurrent.e: Loop diuretics stop NaCl transport in the TAL, which drives the countercurrent multiplier, so the medullary gradient collapses and urine becomes near-isosmotic. Plasma ADH is high, so release is not the problem.

renal-ch28:urea.q: Increased medullary blood flow tends to:
Urea moves from collecting ducts into the thin limbs, a process called:
renal-ch28:urea.e: Traps urea in the inner medulla.

renal-ch28:urea.q: A 30-year-old man with primary polydipsia has been drinking about 10 L/day for months. During a supervised water deprivation test, urine osmolality reaches only 600 mOsm/kg despite high ADH. What best explains the impaired concentrating ability?
o: Washout of medullary solute by high flow
Loss of nephrons from interstitial fibrosis
renal-ch28:urea.e: Chronic high water flow increases medullary blood and tubular flow, washing out NaCl and urea from the interstitium and lowering maximal urine osmolality. ADH is high, so the hypothalamic and receptor options do not fit.

renal-ch28:concentrate.q: Urine flow 2 mL/min, Uosm 150, Posm 300. Free water clearance is:
Central diabetes insipidus is distinguished from nephrogenic DI by:
renal-ch28:concentrate.e: Central DI responds to ADH analog.

renal-ch28:concentrate.q: A 26-year-old man has passed 8 L of urine per day since a head injury. Serum Na⁺ is 149 mEq/L. Urine osmolality is 90 mOsm/kg after water deprivation and rises to 480 mOsm/kg after desmopressin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
renal-ch28:concentrate.e: Failure to concentrate urine with water deprivation, followed by a large rise after desmopressin, indicates ADH deficiency (central DI), here after head trauma. Nephrogenic DI does not respond to desmopressin.

renal-ch28:adh.q: ADH secretion is most sensitive to:
renal-ch28:adh.e: Osmoreceptors respond to ~1% changes; volume must fall ~10% to strongly stimulate ADH.

renal-ch28:adh.q: Free water clearance is negative when:
renal-ch28:adh.e: CH₂O = V − Cosm; concentrated urine means water is being conserved.
Alcohol and clonidine inhibit; nausea, morphine, nicotine and hypoxia stimulate.

renal-ch28:adh.q: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus is caused by:
o: Failure of the kidney to respond to ADH
Lack of ADH from the posterior pituitary
Excess ADH from an ectopic source
Excess aldosterone from an adrenal adenoma
renal-ch28:adh.e: V2 receptor/AQP2 defects or drugs like lithium.

renal-ch28:adh.q: The obligatory urine volume in a person excreting 600 mOsm/day with maximal concentration 1200 mOsm/L is:
A 25-year-old woman loses about 25% of her blood volume in a car crash. Her plasma osmolality is normal, yet her plasma ADH is markedly elevated. This ADH release is mediated mainly by:
o: Baroreceptor input from low blood volume
Angiotensin II inhibition of the hypothalamus
renal-ch28:adh.e: A volume or pressure fall of more than about 10% strongly stimulates ADH through arterial baroreceptors and atrial receptors, even when osmolality is normal. Osmoreceptors respond to small rises in osmolality, which is normal here.

renal-ch29:potassium.q: Which of the following shifts K⁺ INTO cells, causing hypokalemia?
renal-ch29:potassium.e: Insulin, β-agonists, alkalosis and hypo-osmolarity shift K⁺ in. ↓ Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase activity, acidosis and lysis shift K⁺ out.

renal-ch29:potassium.q: Digoxin toxicity can cause hyperkalemia by:
renal-ch29:potassium.e: Blocking the pump leaves K⁺ outside cells.

o: Increasing renal K⁺ excretion via ROMK
Stimulating Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase to move K⁺ into cells
Blocking ROMK channels in the collecting duct
renal-ch29:potassium.e: Used acutely with glucose in hyperkalemia.

renal-ch29:potassium.q: Which shifts K⁺ OUT of cells?
renal-ch29:potassium.e: Also acidosis, cell lysis and strenuous exercise.

renal-ch29:potassium.q: A 19-year-old with type 1 diabetes has DKA, with glucose 520 mg/dL and K⁺ 5.9 mEq/L. After IV insulin, his K⁺ falls to 3.1 mEq/L. Before treatment, his elevated K⁺ reflected:
o: Shift of K⁺ out of cells
renal-ch29:potassium.e: Insulin deficiency and hyperosmolarity (solvent drag) shift K⁺ out of cells, so serum K⁺ is high even though total body K⁺ is depleted by osmotic diuresis. Insulin then drives K⁺ back into cells and unmasks the deficit.

renal-ch29:capimg.q: ECG shows peaked T waves, wide QRS and arrhythmia risk. The electrolyte disturbance is:
renal-ch29:capimg.e: Hypokalemia gives U waves and flat T waves; hypocalcemia prolongs QT.

renal-ch29:capimg.q: Overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia risks:
renal-ch29:capimg.e: Correcting hyponatremia too fast causes osmotic demyelination ('from low to high, your pons will die'). Correcting hypernatremia too fast causes cerebral edema.

renal-ch29:capimg.q: Hypomagnesemia makes hypokalemia refractory because Mg²⁺ normally:
o: Inhibits ROMK K⁺ secretion in the distal nephron
Blocks aldosterone synthesis in the adrenal zona glomerulosa
Stimulates insulin release from β cells
Activates ENaC in the collecting duct
renal-ch29:capimg.e: Low Mg²⁺ removes the brake on ROMK, so renal K⁺ wasting continues until Mg²⁺ is replaced.

renal-ch29:capimg.q: About what fraction of plasma calcium is ionized (the physiologically active form)?
renal-ch29:capimg.e: ~50% ionized, ~40% bound to plasma proteins, ~10% complexed with anions; ionized + complexed are filterable.

renal-ch29:capimg.q: Which diuretic decreases urinary Ca²⁺ excretion?
renal-ch29:capimg.e: Thiazides enhance distal Ca²⁺ reabsorption; loop diuretics increase calcium loss.

renal-ch29:capimg.q: Most filtered Mg²⁺ is reabsorbed in the:
renal-ch29:capimg.e: The TAL reabsorbs ~65% of filtered magnesium (paracellular).

renal-ch29:capimg.q: A 22-year-old woman having a panic attack is breathing rapidly and develops perioral tingling and carpopedal spasm. Her total serum calcium is normal. What best explains her symptoms?
o: ↓ Total body Ca²⁺ from bone deposition
renal-ch29:capimg.e: Respiratory alkalosis frees negative binding sites on albumin, which then bind more Ca²⁺, lowering the ionized fraction while total calcium is unchanged. Changes in PTH or renal handling are too slow to explain acute symptoms.

renal-ch29:volume.q: Long-term arterial pressure is set mainly by:
renal-ch29:volume.e: The renal-body fluid feedback (pressure natriuresis): pressure settles where renal output equals intake on the renal function curve.

o: Spontaneous regression of the adrenal adenoma
Na⁺ excretion normalizing despite high aldosterone
Loss of aldosterone's K⁺-wasting effect over time
renal-ch29:volume.e: Na⁺ excretion returns to normal despite continued aldosterone excess: rising arterial pressure causes pressure natriuresis that offsets Na⁺ retention; hypokalemia persists.

renal-ch29:volume.q: If angiotensin II cannot be suppressed during a high-salt diet, the result is:
o: No change in arterial pressure or volume
renal-ch29:volume.e: The renal function curve flattens; higher pressure is needed to excrete the salt.

renal-ch29:volume.q: ANP is released in response to:
renal-ch29:volume.e: ANP increases Na⁺ excretion and inhibits renin; its role is modest.

renal-ch29:volume.q: A healthy 30-year-old man increases his sodium intake from 50 to 200 mmol/day. Within 3–4 days, his sodium excretion matches intake with only a small rise in ECF volume and almost no change in arterial pressure. What mainly prevents a rise in blood pressure?
renal-ch29:volume.e: A high salt intake suppresses renin and angiotensin II, which lowers Na⁺ reabsorption and lets the kidney excrete the load with minimal pressure rise. If angiotensin II stayed high, the pressure would become salt-sensitive.

renal-ch29:raas.q: Renin is released from juxtaglomerular cells in response to all EXCEPT:
o: Increased NaCl delivery to the macula densa
Decreased NaCl delivery to the macula densa
renal-ch29:raas.e: Renin rises with ↓ perfusion, β₁ stimulation and ↓ NaCl at the macula densa. ↑ NaCl delivery suppresses it.

renal-ch29:raas.q: Angiotensin II acts on the proximal tubule to:
renal-ch29:raas.e: AT II stimulates NHE3 → ↑ Na⁺, HCO₃⁻ and water reabsorption (can cause contraction alkalosis); it also constricts the efferent arteriole, releases aldosterone and ADH, and drives thirst.

renal-ch29:raas.q: ACE also degrades which vasodilator, explaining cough and angioedema with ACE inhibitors?

A 35-year-old woman has a BP of 172/104 mmHg, an epigastric bruit and a 'string of beads' appearance of the right renal artery on angiography. Her plasma renin activity is elevated. Why is renin increased?
o: ↑ NaCl delivery sensed by macula densa
↓ Afferent pressure sensed by JG cells
renal-ch29:raas.e: Fibromuscular dysplasia narrows the renal artery, so the intrarenal baroreceptor (JG cells) senses low afferent pressure and secretes renin. Increased NaCl at the macula densa suppresses renin.

renal-ch30:buffers.q: pH 7.25, PaCO₂ 28, HCO₃⁻ 12. Expected PaCO₂ by Winter's formula is ~26 ± 2. This is:
o: Primary respiratory alkalosis with renal compensation
Metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation
Metabolic acidosis with concurrent respiratory acidosis
renal-ch30:buffers.e: Winter's: 1.5(12) + 8 = 26 ± 2; measured 28 is within range, so compensation is appropriate.

renal-ch30:buffers.q: Which causes a HIGH anion gap metabolic acidosis?
renal-ch30:buffers.e: MUDPILES-type causes (methanol, uremia, DKA, propylene glycol, iron/INH, lactate, ethylene glycol, salicylates). Diarrhea, RTA, acetazolamide → normal AG.

renal-ch30:buffers.q: Vomiting causes metabolic alkalosis that is maintained by:
o: Volume contraction → ↑ aldosterone and AT II
renal-ch30:buffers.e: Loss of HCl and volume; RAAS keeps HCO₃⁻ reabsorption high (saline-responsive alkalosis).

renal-ch30:buffers.q: A 9-year-old has had 3 days of profuse watery diarrhea. Labs: pH 7.29, PaCO₂ 30 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 14 mEq/L, Na⁺ 138, Cl⁻ 114 mEq/L. Which is the best description of the acid–base status?
o: High anion gap acidosis with respiratory alkalosis
Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis, compensated
Normal anion gap acidosis with respiratory acidosis
High anion gap metabolic acidosis, compensated
renal-ch30:buffers.e: The anion gap is 138 − (114 + 14) = 10 (normal), as expected from GI HCO₃⁻ loss, and Winter's formula predicts PaCO₂ 1.5 × 14 + 8 = 29 ± 2, so compensation is appropriate. A PaCO₂ above that range would indicate a coexisting respiratory acidosis.

renal-ch30:resp.q: Doubling alveolar ventilation raises pH by about:
Respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis is incomplete because:
o: Stimulus fades as pH approaches normal
CO₂ cannot act as a buffer

renal-ch30:resp.q: A 30-year-old woman has vomited repeatedly for 4 days. ABG: pH 7.50, HCO₃⁻ 36 mEq/L, PaCO₂ 48 mmHg. The PaCO₂ of 48 mmHg best reflects:
o: Compensation that has fully normalized pH
renal-ch30:resp.e: In metabolic alkalosis, expected PaCO₂ ≈ 40 + 0.7 × (36 − 24) ≈ 48 mmHg, so hypoventilation here is appropriate compensation. Compensation never returns pH fully to normal, and pH 7.50 is still alkalemic.

o: Fanconi syndrome with glucosuria and aminoaciduria
Urine pH > 5.5, hypokalemia, calcium phosphate stones
renal-ch30:renalacid.e: Defect in α-intercalated cell H⁺ secretion; causes include amphotericin B, analgesic nephropathy, autoimmune disease.
Hyperkalemia ↓ ammoniagenesis → ↓ acid excretion; urine pH < 5.5. Causes: diabetes (hyporeninemic), ACE-I, ARBs, K⁺-sparing diuretics.

o: Amphotericin B toxicity to collecting ducts
renal-ch30:renalacid.e: Defective PCT HCO₃⁻ reabsorption; urine pH < 5.5 once plasma HCO₃⁻ is depleted. Hypokalemia.

renal-ch30:renalacid.q: The kidneys must reabsorb about how much HCO₃⁻ per day?
New HCO₃⁻ is added to the blood when secreted H⁺ combines with:
renal-ch30:renalacid.e: Titratable acid and ammonium excretion generate new bicarbonate.

renal-ch30:renalacid.q: In chronic acidosis, the most adaptable renal mechanism is:
renal-ch30:renalacid.e: NH₄⁺ production can rise from ~50 to ~500 mEq/day.

renal-ch30:renalacid.q: Primary active H⁺ secretion that can lower urine pH to 4.5 occurs in:
renal-ch30:renalacid.e: H⁺-ATPase and H⁺/K⁺-ATPase create a ~900-fold gradient.

o: Decreased H⁺ secretion and metabolic acidosis
No effect on renal H⁺ or HCO₃⁻ handling
Increased H⁺ secretion and metabolic alkalosis
renal-ch30:renalacid.e: Table 30-2: hypokalemia stimulates H⁺ secretion and HCO₃⁻ reabsorption.

renal-ch30:renalacid.q: A 36-year-old woman with Sjögren syndrome has recurrent calcium phosphate stones. Labs show K⁺ 3.0 mEq/L and a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis, while urine pH is 6.5. Which transporter is functionally defective?
renal-ch30:renalacid.e: Distal (type 1) RTA, which is associated with Sjögren syndrome, reflects failure of α-intercalated cells to secrete H⁺, so urine pH cannot fall below 5.5. A defect in proximal H⁺ secretion/HCO₃⁻ reabsorption causes type 2 RTA, in which urine can still be acidified.

renal-ch30:ammonia.q: In the PCT, each glutamine metabolized yields:
renal-ch30:ammonia.e: NH₄⁺ to lumen, new HCO₃⁻ to blood.

o: Total H⁺ secreted by the proximal tubule
renal-ch30:ammonia.e: Each unit generates one new HCO₃⁻.

renal-ch30:ammonia.q: Titratable acid mainly reflects H⁺ bound to:
renal-ch30:ammonia.e: HPO₄²⁻ + H⁺ → H₂PO₄⁻. Titratable acid is measured by titrating urine back to pH 7.4.

renal-ch30:ammonia.q: A 63-year-old man with diabetic nephropathy (eGFR 45) has K⁺ 5.8 mEq/L, a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis and a urine pH of 5.0. Low renin and aldosterone are found. His acidosis is mainly due to:
renal-ch30:ammonia.e: In type 4 RTA, hypoaldosteronism causes hyperkalemia, which suppresses proximal ammoniagenesis and lowers NH₄⁺ excretion, so net acid excretion falls even though urine pH can drop below 5.5. Distal H⁺ secretion failure (type 1) gives a urine pH above 5.5.

renal-ch30:abd.q: Which disorder causes hypertension with ↑ renin and ↑ aldosterone?
renal-ch30:abd.e: Low renal perfusion activates RAAS. Primary hyperaldosteronism has ↑ aldosterone but ↓ renin.

renal-ch30:abd.q: Hypertension with ↑ aldosterone and ↓ renin suggests:
renal-ch30:abd.e: Autonomous aldosterone suppresses renin; hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis are common.
Reduced perfusion → renin ↑ → Ang II and aldosterone ↑.

o: Normal BP, hyperkalemia, high renin and aldosterone
Hypotension, hyperkalemia, high renin, low aldosterone
Hypertension, hypokalemia, low renin and low aldosterone
Hypertension, hypokalemia, high renin and aldosterone
renal-ch30:abd.e: ENaC gain of function mimics hyperaldosteronism with suppressed RAAS.

renal-ch30:abd.q: A 17-year-old girl with self-induced vomiting has pH 7.52, HCO₃⁻ 38 mEq/L, K⁺ 2.9 mEq/L and a urine chloride of 8 mEq/L. Which treatment best corrects her acid–base disorder?
renal-ch30:abd.e: A low urine Cl⁻ indicates saline-responsive (chloride-depleted) metabolic alkalosis, maintained by volume contraction and hypokalemia; restoring Cl⁻, volume and K⁺ lets the kidney excrete HCO₃⁻. Spironolactone is used for saline-resistant, mineralocorticoid-driven alkalosis.

renal-ch31:diuretics.q: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors act mainly in the:

o: Exerting an osmotic effect in the tubule
Blocking NCC in the distal tubule
renal-ch31:diuretics.e: It competes with aldosterone at the mineralocorticoid receptor; K⁺-sparing.

renal-ch31:diuretics.q: The natriuretic effect of a diuretic diminishes after a few days because:
o: GFR rises and outstrips the drug's tubular effect
The drug is excreted more rapidly
renal-ch31:diuretics.e: Reduced ECF volume activates compensatory Na⁺ retention via RAAS and sympathetic activation (Guyton Ch 31).

renal-ch31:diuretics.q: A 49-year-old man has hypertension, K⁺ 3.0 mEq/L, high aldosterone with suppressed renin, and bilateral adrenal hyperplasia on imaging. Surgery is not indicated. Which drug is the treatment of choice?
renal-ch31:diuretics.e: Bilateral hyperaldosteronism is treated medically with a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (spironolactone or eplerenone). Amiloride blocks ENaC and is an alternative, but it does not block the aldosterone receptor.

renal-ch31:aki.q: Prerenal acute kidney injury is caused by:
In ATN the tubular epithelium can regenerate in 10–20 days if:
A life-threatening effect of anuria lasting more than a few days is:
renal-ch31:aki.e: Death can occur within 8–14 days without treatment.

renal-ch31:aki.q: A 72-year-old man has prolonged hypotension during cardiac surgery and becomes oliguric. Urine shows muddy brown granular casts; urine Na⁺ is 45 mEq/L, FENa 3% and urine osmolality 310 mOsm/kg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
renal-ch31:aki.e: Muddy brown casts, FENa above 2% and isosthenuric urine show that the tubules cannot conserve Na⁺ or concentrate urine, which is ischemic ATN. Prerenal azotemia has FENa below 1% and concentrated urine.

renal-ch31:ckd.q: The two leading causes of end-stage renal disease are:
The 'vicious cycle' of CKD is driven by:
renal-ch31:ckd.e: Surviving nephrons hypertrophy and hyperfilter; increased glomerular pressure leads to sclerosis.

renal-ch31:ckd.q: Anemia in CKD is mainly due to:
Isosthenuria in advanced CKD means urine osmolality is fixed near:
renal-ch31:ckd.e: Remaining nephrons can neither dilute nor concentrate well.
Reduced 1,25-(OH)₂D₃ and phosphate retention with secondary hyperparathyroidism: renal osteodystrophy.

renal-ch31:ckd.q: A 61-year-old woman with stage 4 CKD has bone pain. Labs: Ca²⁺ 8.0 mg/dL, phosphate 6.4 mg/dL, PTH 480 pg/mL. What is the main mechanism of her elevated PTH?
renal-ch31:ckd.e: In CKD, phosphate retention and reduced 1α-hydroxylation (low calcitriol) lower ionized Ca²⁺ and directly stimulate the parathyroids (secondary hyperparathyroidism). An adenoma causes hypercalcemia with hypophosphatemia.

renal-ch31:tubular.q: A child has hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, hypercalciuria and normal BP. The defect affects which transporter?
o: NCC in the distal convoluted tubule (Gitelman)
NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb (Bartter)
renal-ch31:tubular.e: Bartter mimics loop diuretics: hypokalemic alkalosis with HYPERcalciuria.

renal-ch31:tubular.q: Hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, hypomagnesemia and HYPOcalciuria point to:
renal-ch31:tubular.e: Gitelman = NCC defect in the DCT, mimicking thiazides (hypocalciuria). It is milder than Bartter.

renal-ch31:tubular.q: Hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis with LOW aldosterone that responds to amiloride:
renal-ch31:tubular.e: Gain-of-function ENaC (↓ degradation) → Na⁺ retention with suppressed renin and aldosterone. Treat with amiloride.

renal-ch31:tubular.q: Generalized PCT reabsorption defect with glucosuria, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia and type 2 RTA is:
renal-ch31:tubular.e: Causes include Wilson disease, ifosfamide, cisplatin, expired tetracyclines, multiple myeloma and lead.

renal-ch31:tubular.q: A 24-year-old woman has muscle cramps and fatigue. BP is normal. Labs: K⁺ 2.9 mEq/L, HCO₃⁻ 30 mEq/L, Mg²⁺ 1.2 mg/dL, with low urinary calcium. Her condition mimics the chronic effect of which drug?
renal-ch31:tubular.e: Gitelman syndrome (an NCC defect in the DCT) mimics thiazide or thiazide-like (chlorthalidone) use: hypokalemic alkalosis, hypomagnesemia and hypocalciuria. Bartter syndrome mimics furosemide and causes hypercalciuria.

harrison-ch321:aki-dx.q: RBC casts in the urine point to:
harrison-ch321:aki-dx.e: RBC casts = glomerular bleeding (nephritic syndrome, vasculitis, malignant hypertension).

harrison-ch321:aki-dx.q: Muddy brown granular casts are characteristic of:
harrison-ch321:aki-dx.e: Granular casts come from sloughed tubular cells. Waxy (broad) casts suggest advanced CKD. WBC casts suggest pyelonephritis or interstitial nephritis.

harrison-ch321:aki-dx.q: WBC casts distinguish acute pyelonephritis from:
harrison-ch321:aki-dx.e: Casts form in tubules, so they indicate upper-tract (renal) inflammation, not bladder infection.

harrison-ch321:aki-dx.q: A 62-year-old man is admitted with septic shock requiring norepinephrine for 2 days. His creatinine rises from 1.0 to 3.4 mg/dL, urine sodium is 58 mEq/L and FENa is 3.1%. Urine microscopy will most likely show:
o: Red blood cell casts with dysmorphic RBCs
White blood cell casts with eosinophils
harrison-ch321:aki-dx.e: Prolonged hypotension causes ischemic ATN: FENa > 2% and muddy brown granular casts from sloughed tubular cells. Bland hyaline casts with FENa < 1% fit prerenal azotemia.

o: Pyuria with WBC casts, fever and flank pain
Isolated microscopic hematuria with normal function
Hematuria with RBC casts, hypertension and oliguria
Proteinuria > 3.5 g/day with hypoalbuminemia and edema
robbins-ch20:glomresp.e: Nephrotic = podocyte damage: proteinuria > 3.5 g/day, hypoalbuminemia, edema, hyperlipidemia. Nephritic = inflammation (hematuria, RBC casts, HTN, azotemia).

robbins-ch20:glomresp.q: Nephrotic patients are hypercoagulable mainly because they lose:
robbins-ch20:glomresp.e: Urinary antithrombin loss → thrombosis risk (e.g., renal vein thrombosis, especially in membranous nephropathy).

o: Hyperlipidemia with fatty casts and oval fat bodies
Proteinuria > 3.5 g/day with hypoalbuminemia and edema
Hematuria with RBC casts, hypertension and oliguria
Pyuria with WBC casts and urine eosinophils
robbins-ch20:glomresp.e: Inflammation damages the GBM, letting RBCs through.

robbins-ch20:glomresp.q: 'Spike and dome' on EM with subepithelial deposits suggests:
A 38-year-old man has periorbital and leg edema. Urine protein is 7.2 g/24 h, serum albumin 1.9 g/dL and total cholesterol 390 mg/dL. His hyperlipidemia is best explained by:
o: Reduced bile acid loss in the stool
robbins-ch20:glomresp.e: In nephrotic syndrome low oncotic pressure drives hepatic lipoprotein synthesis (with impaired lipid catabolism). Lipids are not lost in urine in amounts that explain the picture; lipiduria is a consequence, not the cause.

robbins-ch20:psgn.q: Two weeks after impetigo, a 7-year-old has cola-colored urine and periorbital edema. Complement shows:
robbins-ch20:psgn.e: Poststreptococcal GN is immune complex–mediated with ↓ C3; most children recover fully.

robbins-ch20:psgn.q: Anti-GBM antibodies against type IV collagen α3 with linear IF and hemoptysis is:
robbins-ch20:psgn.e: Type II hypersensitivity; linear IgG on IF; RPGN with pulmonary hemorrhage.

robbins-ch20:psgn.q: Gross hematuria 1–2 days after a URI with mesangial IgA deposits is:
robbins-ch20:psgn.e: Synpharyngitic hematuria (days, not weeks). Most common GN worldwide; related to IgA vasculitis.

robbins-ch20:psgn.q: Hereditary nephritis with sensorineural deafness and lens dislocation is:
robbins-ch20:psgn.e: Type IV collagen defect (often X-linked); 'basket-weave' GBM splitting on EM. Can't see, can't pee, can't hear a bee.

robbins-ch20:psgn.q: A 9-year-old boy has smoky urine and periorbital edema 3 weeks after a skin infection. BP is 150/95 mm Hg, urine shows RBC casts and serum C3 is low. Electron microscopy of a kidney biopsy would most likely show:
o: Ribbon-like deposits within the lamina densa
Diffuse effacement of foot processes only
robbins-ch20:psgn.e: Poststreptococcal GN shows subepithelial 'humps' of immune complexes. Ribbon-like intramembranous deposits are dense deposit disease (C3 glomerulopathy).

robbins-ch20:nephrotic.q: Most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children; EM shows effaced foot processes and light microscopy is normal:
robbins-ch20:nephrotic.e: Selective albuminuria, excellent response to corticosteroids; may follow infection, vaccine or Hodgkin lymphoma.

robbins-ch20:nephrotic.q: Anti-PLA2R antibodies with spike-and-dome subepithelial deposits indicate:
robbins-ch20:nephrotic.e: Most common primary nephrotic cause in white adults. Secondary causes: SLE, hepatitis B/C, NSAIDs, solid tumors.

robbins-ch20:nephrotic.q: Nephrotic syndrome in a patient with HIV, heroin use or sickle cell disease is most likely:
robbins-ch20:nephrotic.e: FSGS: segmental sclerosis; most common primary nephrotic cause in Black and Hispanic adults. HIV causes the collapsing variant.

robbins-ch20:nephrotic.q: A 34-year-old man who injects heroin has 5.8 g/day proteinuria, serum albumin 2.4 g/dL, BP 152/94 mm Hg and creatinine 1.6 mg/dL. Light microscopy of a kidney biopsy would most likely show:
o: Diffuse GBM thickening with silver spikes
Sclerosis of portions of some glomeruli
robbins-ch20:nephrotic.e: Heroin use is a classic secondary cause of FSGS: segmental sclerosis in a subset of glomeruli. Normal light microscopy would point to minimal change disease.

robbins-ch20:stones.q: The most common type of kidney stone is:
robbins-ch20:stones.e: Calcium stones (oxalate > phosphate) are most common; risks include hypercalciuria and low citrate.

robbins-ch20:stones.q: Staghorn calculi in alkaline urine with a urease-positive organism are made of:
robbins-ch20:stones.e: Struvite (ammonium magnesium phosphate). Proteus, Klebsiella, Staph saprophyticus split urea → NH₃ → alkaline urine. Treat infection and remove stone.

robbins-ch20:stones.q: Radiolucent stones forming in acidic urine in a patient with gout or tumor lysis are:
robbins-ch20:stones.e: Not visible on X-ray (visible on CT/US); treat with urine alkalinization and allopurinol.

robbins-ch20:stones.q: Hexagonal crystals and a positive cyanide-nitroprusside test indicate:
robbins-ch20:stones.e: Cystinuria (defective COLA transporter in PCT) — treat with alkalinization, hydration, chelating agents.

robbins-ch20:stones.q: A 41-year-old woman with Crohn disease who had 90 cm of ileum resected has recurrent calcium oxalate stones. 24-hour urine shows high oxalate with normal calcium. The main mechanism is:
o: Unbound oxalate absorbed as fat binds calcium
robbins-ch20:stones.e: Fat malabsorption leaves luminal calcium bound to fatty acids, so free oxalate is absorbed in the colon (enteric hyperoxaluria). Hepatic oxalate overproduction is primary hyperoxaluria, a genetic disorder.

robbins-ch20:obstruction.q: Hydronephrosis is dilation of the renal pelvis and calyces most often due to:
robbins-ch20:obstruction.e: Causes: stones, BPH, cervical cancer, PUV, pregnancy. Prolonged pressure causes cortical atrophy.

robbins-ch20:obstruction.q: Bilateral hydronephrosis in an older man with nocturia and weak stream suggests:
robbins-ch20:obstruction.e: Bladder outlet obstruction affects both kidneys; unilateral hydronephrosis suggests an obstruction above the bladder.

robbins-ch20:obstruction.q: Unilateral hydronephrosis from a stone usually:
o: Causes anuria and acute kidney failure
robbins-ch20:obstruction.e: The contralateral kidney compensates, so creatinine stays near normal. Bilateral obstruction or a single kidney is needed for renal failure.
Pressure transmitted back causes compression atrophy of the cortex and medulla.

robbins-ch20:obstruction.q: A 74-year-old man with weak stream and nocturia has a post-void residual of 900 mL, bilateral hydronephrosis and creatinine 2.9 mg/dL. The earliest functional derangement caused by this process is:
o: Red blood cell casts in the urine
robbins-ch20:obstruction.e: Early obstruction mainly damages tubular function, so concentrating ability falls first (polyuria, nocturia). Glomerular findings such as heavy proteinuria or RBC casts are not features of obstruction.

robbins-ch21:cystitis.q: The most common cause of acute cystitis is:
robbins-ch21:cystitis.e: E. coli is most common; S. saprophyticus is the second most common cause in sexually active young women.

robbins-ch21:cystitis.q: A positive leukocyte esterase test indicates:
robbins-ch21:cystitis.e: Nitrite test detects gram-negative bacteria (nitrate reductase). Sterile pyuria suggests urethritis (Chlamydia, gonorrhea).

o: Hemoglobin or red cells in the urine
robbins-ch21:cystitis.e: Gram-negative bacteria (E. coli and other Enterobacteriaceae) convert nitrate to nitrite.
WBCs without growth on standard culture.

robbins-ch21:cystitis.q: A renal transplant recipient has yellow mucosal plaques in the bladder; macrophages contain laminated calcified Michaelis–Gutmann bodies. Diagnosis:
robbins-ch21:cystitis.e: Malakoplakia: defective phagolysosome function in chronic E. coli infection, more frequent in immunosuppression.
Cytotoxic drugs (cyclophosphamide) and adenovirus/BK virus cause hemorrhagic cystitis.

robbins-ch21:cystitis.q: The main purpose of biopsy in suspected interstitial cystitis is to:

A 21-year-old sexually active woman has dysuria and frequency without fever. Urine nitrite is negative and leukocyte esterase positive; culture grows gram-positive, catalase-positive, coagulase-negative cocci resistant to novobiocin. The organism is:
robbins-ch21:cystitis.e: Novobiocin-resistant coagulase-negative staph in a young sexually active woman is S. saprophyticus, the second most common cause of cystitis. S. epidermidis is novobiocin-sensitive.

robbins-ch20:pyelo.q: Fever, flank pain, CVA tenderness and WBC casts indicate:
robbins-ch20:pyelo.e: Upper-tract infection, usually ascending E. coli; affects cortex with relative glomerular sparing.

robbins-ch20:pyelo.q: Chronic pyelonephritis shows coarse asymmetric corticomedullary scarring and thyroidization of the kidney due to:
robbins-ch20:pyelo.e: Tubules contain eosinophilic casts resembling thyroid follicles.

robbins-ch20:pyelo.q: Chronic pyelonephritis with thyroid-like tubules filled with eosinophilic casts is called:
Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis is classically associated with:
Sloughing of renal papillae with gross hematuria is associated with all EXCEPT:
robbins-ch20:pyelo.e: SAAD papa: Sickle cell, Acute pyelonephritis, Analgesics, Diabetes.

robbins-ch20:pyelo.q: Papillary necrosis is particularly likely because the papillae have:
o: Abundant collateral supply from capsular arteries
Sparse vasa recta supply in a hypertonic milieu
No tubular epithelium, only connective tissue
Direct arterial supply from interlobar arteries
robbins-ch20:pyelo.e: Poor blood supply from the vasa recta plus a hypertonic environment: low O₂ and hypertonicity make the papillae vulnerable (e.g., sickling).

robbins-ch20:pyelo.q: Causes of renal papillary necrosis include:
o: Minimal change disease and IgA nephropathy
Sickle cell disease and analgesic abuse
robbins-ch20:pyelo.e: Mnemonic SAAD: Sickle cell, Acute pyelonephritis, Analgesics, Diabetes.
Sloughed papillae may appear in the urine or cause ureteric obstruction.

robbins-ch20:pyelo.q: A 27-year-old woman has fever of 39.2 °C, right flank pain and costovertebral angle tenderness. Urinalysis shows pyuria, bacteriuria and WBC casts; culture grows Escherichia coli. The infection most likely reached the kidney by:
robbins-ch20:pyelo.e: Acute pyelonephritis is usually ascending: gut flora colonize the urethra and bladder, then reach the kidney (helped by reflux). Hematogenous spread is uncommon and involves organisms like S. aureus.

harrison-ch321:aki-def.q: BUN:Cr > 20 and FENa < 1% in AKI suggest:
harrison-ch321:aki-def.e: Hypoperfusion → kidneys avidly reabsorb Na⁺ and urea. Intrinsic damage gives FENa > 2% and BUN:Cr < 15.

harrison-ch321:aki-def.q: Urine osmolality > 500 mOsm/kg in AKI points to:
harrison-ch321:aki-def.e: Intact tubules still concentrate urine. ATN loses concentrating ability (Uosm < 350).

o: Muddy brown granular casts in urine
FENa < 1% with a normal urine sediment

harrison-ch321:aki-def.e: Tubules work and avidly reabsorb Na⁺ and urea: BUN/Cr > 20, FENa < 1%, high urine osmolality.

harrison-ch321:aki-def.q: A 68-year-old man's creatinine rises from a baseline of 1.0 to 2.3 mg/dL within 48 hours after abdominal surgery. Urine output has been 0.4 mL/kg/h for the past 8 hours. His AKI is classified as:
harrison-ch321:aki-def.e: Creatinine 2.0–2.9 × baseline = stage 2; the urine output (< 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6–12 h) alone would be stage 1, and the higher stage is assigned.

robbins-ch20:tin.q: Fever, rash, eosinophilia and pyuria with WBC casts days after starting a drug suggest:
robbins-ch20:tin.e: Hypersensitivity to drugs (penicillins, PPIs, NSAIDs, diuretics, rifampin, sulfonamides); urine eosinophils.

robbins-ch20:tin.q: First step in managing drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis is:
robbins-ch20:tin.e: Most recover after withdrawal; corticosteroids may help if improvement is slow.

robbins-ch20:tin.q: Drugs commonly causing acute interstitial nephritis include:
robbins-ch20:tin.e: Hypersensitivity (type IV) reaction in the interstitium. Common culprits: penicillins, NSAIDs, PPIs, diuretics, rifampin, sulfonamides.

robbins-ch20:tin.q: A characteristic urine finding in drug-induced AIN is:
o: Fatty casts and oval fat bodies
robbins-ch20:tin.e: Eosinophiluria and WBC casts with fever and rash.

robbins-ch20:tin.q: A 64-year-old woman started omeprazole 3 weeks ago. She now has low-grade fever and a faint rash; creatinine has risen from 0.9 to 2.4 mg/dL and urine shows pyuria with WBC casts. A kidney biopsy would most likely show:
robbins-ch20:tin.e: Drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis: interstitial edema with lymphocytes, macrophages and eosinophils, sparing glomeruli. Crescents indicate RPGN, which presents with RBC casts.

robbins-ch20:atn.q: The most common cause of acute kidney injury in hospitalized patients is:
robbins-ch20:atn.e: Ischemic (shock, sepsis) or nephrotoxic (aminoglycosides, contrast, myoglobin, cisplatin) ATN.

robbins-ch20:atn.q: The maintenance phase of ATN is notable for:
robbins-ch20:atn.e: Maintenance phase: oliguria, hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis. Recovery phase: tubules regenerate → polyuria and risk of hypokalemia.
High O₂ demand in the outer medulla.
Direct tubular toxicity (aminoglycosides, contrast, myoglobin, heavy metals); basement membrane usually preserved so cells regenerate.

robbins-ch20:atn.q: A 60-year-old man receives gentamicin for 10 days for Pseudomonas bacteremia. His creatinine rises from 1.1 to 3.0 mg/dL with granular casts and FENa 2.8%. The nephron segment most directly injured is the:
robbins-ch20:atn.e: Aminoglycosides are taken up by proximal tubular cells and cause nephrotoxic ATN there. Podocyte injury would cause proteinuria, not granular casts with a high FENa.

harrison-ch322:ckd-sys.q: Which consequence of CKD causes a normocytic anemia?
harrison-ch322:ckd-sys.e: CKD: ↓ EPO → anemia; also uremia, HTN, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, volume overload, renal osteodystrophy.

harrison-ch322:ckd-sys.q: Uremia can cause which complication requiring urgent dialysis?
harrison-ch322:ckd-sys.e: Dialysis indications (AEIOU): Acidosis, Electrolytes (K⁺), Intoxication, Overload, Uremic symptoms (pericarditis, encephalopathy).

harrison-ch322:ckd-sys.q: Uremic pericarditis is an indication for:
harrison-ch322:ckd-sys.e: Dialysis indications: AEIOU (acidosis, electrolytes, intoxication, overload, uremia).

harrison-ch322:ckd-sys.q: Hyperkalemia in kidney failure occurs because:
The primary cause of anemia in CKD is:
harrison-ch322:ckd-sys.e: Insufficient erythropoietin production: normocytic anemia from stage 3, almost universal by stage 4.

harrison-ch322:ckd-sys.q: The leading cause of death in CKD is:
harrison-ch322:ckd-sys.e: CVD is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality.

harrison-ch322:ckd-sys.q: Before starting an ESA in CKD you should ensure:
harrison-ch322:ckd-sys.e: Iron (TSAT, ferritin) is needed for response.

harrison-ch322:ckd-sys.q: A 60-year-old woman with CKD stage G4 reports fatigue. Hemoglobin is 8.9 g/dL with normal MCV; ferritin 350 ng/mL, transferrin saturation 30%, B12 and folate normal. The most appropriate treatment is:
harrison-ch322:ckd-sys.e: Anemia of CKD is from erythropoietin deficiency; with iron stores replete, an ESA is indicated. B12 and folate are normal, so replacing them adds nothing.

harrison-ch322:ckd-mbd.q: Renal osteodystrophy develops because CKD causes:
harrison-ch322:ckd-mbd.e: Hypocalcemia + hyperphosphatemia + ↓ vitamin D → ↑ PTH → bone resorption (osteitis fibrosa cystica).

harrison-ch322:ckd-mbd.q: In CKD-mineral bone disease, FGF23 is:
harrison-ch322:ckd-mbd.e: Osteocyte FGF23 rises early to excrete phosphate and inhibits 1α-hydroxylase.

harrison-ch322:ckd-mbd.q: Secondary hyperparathyroidism in CKD is driven by:
harrison-ch322:ckd-mbd.e: Phosphate retention, low calcitriol and the resulting hypocalcemia all stimulate PTH.

harrison-ch322:ckd-mbd.q: Osteitis fibrosa cystica in CKD is due to:
In CKD, the earliest hormonal change in mineral metabolism is a rise in:
harrison-ch322:ckd-mbd.e: FGF-23 rises early in response to phosphate retention.

harrison-ch322:ckd-mbd.q: Adynamic bone disease is associated with:
harrison-ch322:ckd-mbd.e: Low turnover bone disease, increasingly common in diabetics and the elderly.
Vascular calcification with skin necrosis, almost exclusively in advanced CKD; a devastating condition in ESKD patients.

harrison-ch322:ckd-mbd.q: A 58-year-old man on hemodialysis for 6 years has bone pain. Calcium is 8.1 mg/dL, phosphate 7.2 mg/dL and PTH 850 pg/mL; hand films show subperiosteal resorption. A bone biopsy would most likely show:
o: Mosaic lamellar bone with cement lines
Low turnover with very few bone cells
Wide seams of unmineralized osteoid alone
harrison-ch322:ckd-mbd.e: Very high PTH from secondary hyperparathyroidism produces high-turnover osteitis fibrosa cystica. Low turnover with few cells is adynamic bone disease from oversuppressed PTH.

robbins-ch20:cystic.q: Bilateral enlarged kidneys with cysts, hematuria and flank pain in an adult with a family history and berry aneurysms:
robbins-ch20:cystic.e: PKD1 (chr 16) or PKD2 (chr 4). Associations: berry aneurysms, mitral valve prolapse, hepatic cysts, diverticulosis. Tolvaptan slows progression.

robbins-ch20:cystic.q: ARPKD presents in infancy and is associated with:
robbins-ch20:cystic.e: PKHD1 mutation; can cause Potter sequence; survivors develop portal hypertension and hypertension.
PKD1/PKD2 mutations; also mitral valve prolapse.

robbins-ch20:cystic.q: Acquired cystic kidney disease is seen in:
robbins-ch20:cystic.e: Risk of renal cell carcinoma rises.

robbins-ch20:cystic.q: A 36-year-old man has hypertension, intermittent hematuria and bilateral palpable flank masses. His father died of a subarachnoid hemorrhage. The most likely defective protein is encoded on chromosome 16 and is:
robbins-ch20:cystic.e: ADPKD is caused mostly by PKD1 (polycystin-1, chromosome 16); PKD2 (polycystin-2) accounts for the rest. Fibrocystin (PKHD1, chromosome 6) is the ARPKD protein.

robbins-ch20:rcc.q: Renal cell carcinoma (clear cell) arises from which cells?
robbins-ch20:rcc.e: Polygonal clear cells filled with lipid and carbohydrate; associated with VHL gene deletion on chromosome 3.

robbins-ch20:rcc.q: Classic triad of RCC (rarely all present):
o: Hematuria, palpable flank mass and flank pain
robbins-ch20:rcc.e: RCC can secrete EPO (polycythemia), PTHrP (hypercalcemia), renin, ACTH; it may invade the IVC and cause left varicocele.

robbins-ch20:rcc.q: Strongest modifiable risk factor for RCC:
robbins-ch20:rcc.e: Also obesity, male sex, hypertension; von Hippel–Lindau → bilateral RCC.

robbins-ch20:rcc.q: A 63-year-old man who smokes has painless hematuria and a left flank mass. Hemoglobin is 18.6 g/dL. Nephrectomy shows a yellow tumor of cells with clear cytoplasm. The most likely initiating genetic event is:
robbins-ch20:rcc.e: Clear cell RCC begins with loss of the VHL tumor suppressor (3p), which stabilizes HIF and raises VEGF and EPO (hence polycythemia). MET activation drives papillary RCC.

robbins-ch20:benign.q: A renal mass with a central stellate scar and large eosinophilic cells full of mitochondria is:
robbins-ch20:benign.e: Benign tumor from collecting duct intercalated cells; usually removed because it is hard to tell from RCC on imaging.
Benign tumor of intercalated cells, mitochondria-rich.

robbins-ch20:benign.q: On histology, oncocytes are eosinophilic because they contain many:
robbins-ch20:benign.e: Packed mitochondria give granular pink cytoplasm.

robbins-ch20:benign.q: Management of a suspected oncocytoma is usually:
robbins-ch20:benign.e: Usually excised because it cannot reliably be distinguished from RCC (especially chromophobe RCC) preoperatively.

robbins-ch20:benign.q: A 32-year-old woman with seizures and facial angiofibromas has an incidental 3-cm renal mass that contains macroscopic fat on CT. The tumor is composed mainly of:
robbins-ch20:benign.e: Tuberous sclerosis is associated with angiomyolipoma, made of abnormal vessels, smooth muscle and fat. Oncocytes characterize oncocytoma, which contains no fat.

robbins-ch20:wilms.q: Most common renal malignancy of early childhood presenting as a large palpable unilateral flank mass:
robbins-ch20:wilms.e: Ages 2–4; contains embryonic glomerular structures; loss of WT1 or WT2 (chromosome 11).

robbins-ch20:wilms.q: WAGR syndrome includes Wilms tumor, aniridia, genitourinary anomalies and:
robbins-ch20:wilms.e: WT1 deletion. Beckwith–Wiedemann (WT2): macroglossia, organomegaly, hemihyperplasia. Denys–Drash: early nephropathy, DSD.

robbins-ch20:wilms.q: Wilms tumor histology shows a triphasic pattern of:
o: Small round cells with rosettes only

robbins-ch20:wilms.q: WT1 mutations in Denys–Drash syndrome cause Wilms tumor plus:
o: Early nephrotic syndrome and gonadal dysgenesis
Sensorineural hearing loss and lens defects
robbins-ch20:wilms.e: Denys–Drash (WT1 mutation): early nephrotic syndrome from diffuse mesangial sclerosis and male pseudohermaphroditism (gonadal dysgenesis). WAGR = WT1 deletion; Beckwith–Wiedemann = WT2.

robbins-ch20:wilms.q: A 3-year-old boy with a history of omphalocele, macroglossia and right hemihypertrophy has a large left flank mass that does not cross the midline. The underlying genetic defect is most likely:
robbins-ch20:wilms.e: Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome (WT2 locus, imprinting at 11p15.5) predisposes to Wilms tumor. WT1 deletion at 11p13 is WAGR syndrome, which features aniridia.

robbins-ch21:urothelial.q: Urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma most commonly presents with:
robbins-ch21:urothelial.e: Can occur anywhere from pelvis to bladder; often multifocal and recurrent.

robbins-ch21:urothelial.q: Which exposure is most strongly linked to urothelial carcinoma?
robbins-ch21:urothelial.e: Also aromatic amines (dyes, rubber), cyclophosphamide, phenacetin. Schistosomiasis is linked to squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.

robbins-ch21:urothelial.q: Cyclophosphamide increases the risk of bladder cancer via:
robbins-ch21:urothelial.e: Also causes hemorrhagic cystitis; prevented by mesna.

robbins-ch21:urothelial.q: Squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder is associated with:
The most important risk factor for urothelial carcinoma of the bladder is:
robbins-ch21:urothelial.e: Smoking raises risk 3–7×; 50–80% of bladder cancers in men are smoking-associated.

robbins-ch21:urothelial.q: Non-muscle-invasive papillary urothelial tumors commonly carry:
robbins-ch21:urothelial.e: Papillary pathway: FGFR3/RAS/PI3K; frequent recurrence but only ~20% progress to muscle invasion.

robbins-ch21:urothelial.q: Most muscle-invasive bladder cancers arise from:
robbins-ch21:urothelial.e: CIS pathway with early TP53/RB mutations gives rise to most muscle-invasive cancers.

robbins-ch21:urothelial.q: A 64-year-old man who worked 30 years in a dye factory and smokes has painless gross hematuria. Cystoscopy shows a papillary tumor on the lateral bladder wall. Biopsy most likely shows:
robbins-ch21:urothelial.e: Smoking and aromatic amines (aniline dyes) cause urothelial carcinoma, > 90% of bladder cancers. Squamous cell carcinoma is linked to schistosomiasis and chronic irritation.

robbins-ch20:syndromes.q: A patient has BUN and creatinine elevated with nausea, peripheral neuropathy and fibrinous pericarditis. This is best termed:
robbins-ch20:syndromes.e: Uremia = azotemia plus clinical signs and biochemical abnormalities (uremic gastroenteritis, neuropathy, fibrinous pericarditis).

robbins-ch20:syndromes.q: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis is defined clinically by:
o: Nephritic syndrome with GFR loss over weeks
Isolated hematuria 1–2 days after a URI
robbins-ch20:syndromes.e: RPGN = nephritic picture + rapid GFR loss over days–weeks; morphologically crescents in most glomeruli.

robbins-ch20:syndromes.q: A 70-year-old woman with heart failure has BUN 48 mg/dL and creatinine 1.9 mg/dL found on routine labs. She has no nausea, pericarditis, neuropathy or other symptoms. This state is best termed:
robbins-ch20:syndromes.e: Azotemia is a biochemical rise in BUN and creatinine; it becomes uremia only when clinical signs (GI, neuropathy, pericarditis) appear.

robbins-ch20:immune.q: Linear IgG along the GBM on immunofluorescence indicates antibodies against:
o: α3 NC1 domain of type IV collagen
robbins-ch20:immune.e: Anti-GBM disease: in situ antibodies against the α3 chain NC1 domain of type IV collagen produce a linear pattern.

robbins-ch20:immune.q: Why do subepithelial deposits cause little inflammation compared with subendothelial deposits?
o: The GBM separates them from blood leukocytes
They consist of IgA rather than IgG
robbins-ch20:immune.e: Subepithelial deposits sit outside the GBM, away from blood leukocytes, so proteinuria dominates (e.g., membranous).

robbins-ch20:immune.q: Membranous nephropathy in most primary cases is due to autoantibodies against:
robbins-ch20:immune.e: Primary MN: in situ immune complexes with podocyte antigen PLA2R (70–80%), less often THSD7A.

robbins-ch20:immune.q: A 28-year-old woman with SLE has hematuria and 2 g/day proteinuria. Immunofluorescence of a biopsy shows granular IgG and C3 along capillary walls and mesangium. Her glomerular injury is mainly caused by:
o: Antibodies to a collagen IV antigen
robbins-ch20:immune.e: Granular deposits indicate immune complexes, in lupus largely formed in the circulation (DNA–anti-DNA) and trapped in glomeruli. Anti-GBM antibodies give a linear pattern.

robbins-ch20:progression.q: The histologic feature that best predicts decline of GFR in chronic glomerular disease is:
robbins-ch20:progression.e: Tubulointerstitial fibrosis correlates better with loss of renal function than the severity of glomerular injury.

robbins-ch20:progression.q: ACE inhibitors slow progression of CKD mainly by:
robbins-ch20:progression.e: Adaptive hyperfiltration raises glomerular capillary pressure; ACEi/ARB dilate the efferent arteriole and lower it.

robbins-ch20:progression.q: A 45-year-old man lost one kidney in a car accident; the other is scarred from childhood reflux. Years later he has 2.5 g/day proteinuria and rising creatinine. Biopsy of his remaining glomeruli most likely shows:
robbins-ch20:progression.e: Loss of nephron mass causes adaptive hyperfiltration in the remaining glomeruli, leading to secondary FSGS and progressive decline. Normal glomeruli with effacement describes minimal change disease.

robbins-ch20:rpgn.q: Pauci-immune crescentic GN is most often associated with:
robbins-ch20:rpgn.e: Type III (pauci-immune) RPGN: little or no Ig on IF; >90% of idiopathic cases are ANCA-positive (GPA = PR3, MPA = MPO).
Fibrin leakage into Bowman space stimulates parietal epithelial cell proliferation and monocyte/macrophage influx.

robbins-ch20:rpgn.q: Goodpasture syndrome differs from renal-limited anti-GBM disease by the presence of:
robbins-ch20:rpgn.e: Anti-GBM antibodies cross-react with alveolar basement membrane → pulmonary hemorrhage.

robbins-ch20:rpgn.q: A 58-year-old man has chronic sinusitis, hemoptysis and creatinine rising from 1.2 to 4.1 mg/dL over 3 weeks. Biopsy shows crescents in most glomeruli with little immunoglobulin on immunofluorescence. His autoantibody most likely targets:
robbins-ch20:rpgn.e: Sinus, lung and kidney involvement with pauci-immune crescentic GN = granulomatosis with polyangiitis, PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA). MPO-ANCA is typical of microscopic polyangiitis.

robbins-ch20:iga.q: A 20-year-old has gross hematuria 1 day after a sore throat. Biopsy will most likely show:
robbins-ch20:iga.e: Synpharyngitic hematuria = IgA nephropathy; mesangial IgA ± C3. PSGN appears 1–4 weeks later.

robbins-ch20:iga.q: The key abnormal molecule in IgA nephropathy is:
robbins-ch20:iga.e: Galactose-deficient IgA1 elicits autoantibodies forming immune complexes that deposit in the mesangium.

robbins-ch20:iga.q: Henoch–Schönlein purpura shares its renal lesion with:
robbins-ch20:iga.e: HSP (IgA vasculitis) has mesangial IgA deposition identical to IgA nephropathy plus purpura, GI and joint symptoms.

robbins-ch20:iga.q: A 6-year-old boy has palpable purpura over the buttocks and legs, colicky abdominal pain, knee arthralgia and microscopic hematuria 1 week after a cold. A skin biopsy of a lesion would most likely show:
o: Linear IgG along the basement membrane
robbins-ch20:iga.e: Henoch–Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) is a leukocytoclastic small-vessel vasculitis with IgA deposits, sharing its renal lesion with IgA nephropathy.

robbins-ch20:alport.q: A boy with hematuria, sensorineural deafness and lens dislocation most likely has a mutation in:
robbins-ch20:alport.e: Alport syndrome: ~85% X-linked COL4A5; GBM shows splitting/basket-weave.

robbins-ch20:alport.q: Thin basement membrane nephropathy typically presents with:
o: Hearing loss with progression to ESRD
robbins-ch20:alport.e: Benign familial hematuria: heterozygous COL4A3/A4, GBM 150–250 nm, normal function.

robbins-ch20:alport.q: A 19-year-old man has had microscopic hematuria since childhood and now has bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. A maternal uncle is on dialysis. Electron microscopy of a kidney biopsy would most likely show:
o: Dense ribbon-like deposits in the GBM
Splitting and lamination of the lamina densa
Diffuse effacement of foot processes only
robbins-ch20:alport.e: X-linked Alport syndrome (COL4A5) gives an irregularly thickened GBM with splitting into a 'basket-weave' pattern. Subepithelial humps are seen in postinfectious GN.

robbins-ch20:membranous.q: Silver stain showing 'spikes' along the GBM is characteristic of:
robbins-ch20:membranous.e: GBM material grows between subepithelial deposits, forming spikes.

robbins-ch20:membranous.q: A patient with membranous nephropathy develops sudden flank pain and hematuria. The most likely complication is:
robbins-ch20:membranous.e: Nephrotic syndrome (especially MN) is hypercoagulable: loss of antithrombin III → renal vein thrombosis.

robbins-ch20:membranous.q: Which is a cause of secondary membranous nephropathy?
robbins-ch20:membranous.e: Secondary MN: HBV, HCV, syphilis, malaria, solid tumors, SLE, NSAIDs, penicillamine, gold.

robbins-ch20:membranous.q: A 66-year-old man who smokes has 9 kg weight loss and new nephrotic syndrome. Biopsy shows diffuse GBM thickening with subepithelial deposits; serum anti-PLA2R is negative. The most likely underlying cause is:
robbins-ch20:membranous.e: Anti-PLA2R–negative membranous nephropathy in an older smoker with weight loss suggests secondary disease from a solid tumor (lung, colon). Hodgkin lymphoma is linked to minimal change disease.

robbins-ch20:mcd.q: A 4-year-old with nephrotic syndrome; LM normal, IF negative. EM shows:
robbins-ch20:mcd.e: Minimal change disease: only EM change is diffuse foot process effacement.

robbins-ch20:mcd.q: Minimal change disease in adults is classically associated with:
robbins-ch20:mcd.e: MCD is linked to Hodgkin lymphoma, NSAIDs, atopy, recent URI or vaccination.

robbins-ch20:mcd.q: The best predictor of good prognosis in childhood nephrotic syndrome is:
robbins-ch20:mcd.e: >90% of children with MCD respond to steroids; relapses may occur but prognosis is excellent.

robbins-ch20:mcd.q: A 5-year-old boy has periorbital and scrotal edema. Urine protein is 4+ with no hematuria, BP is normal, serum albumin is 1.8 g/dL and complement levels are normal. The most appropriate next step is:
robbins-ch20:mcd.e: A typical child with nephrotic syndrome most likely has minimal change disease and is treated with steroids without biopsy. Biopsy is reserved for steroid resistance or atypical features.

robbins-ch20:fsgs.q: Collapsing glomerulopathy with tubular microcysts is classically seen in:
robbins-ch20:fsgs.e: HIVAN: collapsing variant of FSGS with podocyte hyperplasia and microcystic tubules.

robbins-ch20:fsgs.q: APOL1 risk variants increase the risk of FSGS in people of:
robbins-ch20:fsgs.e: APOL1 variants on chromosome 22 are common in African ancestry and raise risk of FSGS and nondiabetic CKD.

robbins-ch20:fsgs.q: Compared with minimal change disease, FSGS more often shows:
o: Hematuria, hypertension and poor steroid response
robbins-ch20:fsgs.e: FSGS: nonselective proteinuria, hematuria, HT, poor steroid response, ~50% ESRD in 10 years.

robbins-ch20:fsgs.q: A 40-year-old man has nephrotic syndrome with hematuria and hypertension that does not respond to 12 weeks of prednisone. Light microscopy shows sclerosis in part of some glomeruli. Immunofluorescence would most likely show:
o: IgM and C3 in sclerotic segments
robbins-ch20:fsgs.e: In FSGS, IgM and C3 are trapped nonspecifically in sclerotic segments; this is not an immune complex disease. Granular IgG with PLA2R is membranous nephropathy.

robbins-ch20:mpgn.q: 'Tram-track' double contour of capillary walls results from:
o: Amyloid fibril deposition in the wall
robbins-ch20:mpgn.e: In MPGN, mesangial cells extend into the capillary wall and lay down new BM → duplicated contour.

robbins-ch20:mpgn.q: Dense deposit disease is caused by:
o: COL4A5 mutation in type IV collagen
robbins-ch20:mpgn.e: C3 glomerulopathy: C3NeF stabilizes C3 convertase → low C3 and C3-only deposits.

robbins-ch20:mpgn.q: Secondary immune-complex MPGN is most classically associated with:
robbins-ch20:mpgn.e: Chronic HCV (± cryoglobulins), HBV, endocarditis, SLE and CLL/lymphoma cause MPGN.

robbins-ch20:mpgn.q: A 48-year-old woman with hepatitis C has palpable purpura, arthralgia, hematuria with RBC casts and 3 g/day proteinuria. C4 is low and serum cryoglobulins are present. Light microscopy of a kidney biopsy would most likely show:
robbins-ch20:mpgn.e: HCV-related cryoglobulinemia causes immune-complex MPGN with lobular glomeruli and double-contoured ('tram-track') GBM. Spikes are membranous nephropathy.

robbins-ch20:lupus.q: The most common and most severe class of lupus nephritis is:
robbins-ch20:lupus.e: Diffuse proliferative (≥50% glomeruli) with subendothelial deposits and wire loops.

robbins-ch20:lupus.q: 'Wire loop' lesions in lupus are due to:
robbins-ch20:lupus.e: Massive subendothelial deposits thicken capillary walls → wire loops on LM.

robbins-ch20:lupus.q: Lupus class V nephritis presents mainly as:
robbins-ch20:lupus.e: Class V = membranous lupus nephritis with subepithelial deposits → nephrotic syndrome.

robbins-ch20:lupus.q: A 26-year-old woman with SLE has RBC casts, 2.5 g/day proteinuria, rising creatinine, low C3 and C4 and high anti-dsDNA. Biopsy shows endocapillary proliferation in 70% of glomeruli with wire loops. The best initial treatment is:
robbins-ch20:lupus.e: Class IV (diffuse) lupus nephritis requires induction immunosuppression: glucocorticoids with mycophenolate (or cyclophosphamide). Hydroxychloroquine is background therapy, not induction.

robbins-ch20:diabetic.q: The earliest morphologic change of diabetic nephropathy on EM is:
robbins-ch20:diabetic.e: GBM thickening is the earliest change; nodules come later.
Involvement of efferent arterioles is characteristic of diabetes.
Nodular glomerulosclerosis in diabetes: PAS-positive nodules of mesangial matrix.

robbins-ch20:diabetic.q: A 57-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 18 years has retinopathy and 2 g/day albuminuria. Biopsy shows nodular PAS-positive mesangial lesions and hyaline arteriolosclerosis. These changes are mainly driven by:
robbins-ch20:diabetic.e: Chronic hyperglycemia forms advanced glycation end products that cross-link matrix, thickening the GBM and expanding the mesangium (Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodules). Light-chain deposition is a nodular mimic in myeloma.

robbins-ch20:systemic.q: Glomerular deposits that show apple-green birefringence with Congo red under polarized light are:
robbins-ch20:systemic.e: Amyloid fibrils 7.5–10 nm; fibrillary GN fibrils are larger and Congo red–negative.

robbins-ch20:systemic.q: Minimal change disease associated with a tumor is classically linked to:
robbins-ch20:systemic.e: Table 20.10: carcinomas → membranous; Hodgkin → MCD; leukemia/lymphoma → MPGN.

robbins-ch20:systemic.q: A 62-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis for 15 years develops nephrotic syndrome. A biopsy shows glomerular deposits with apple-green birefringence on Congo red. The deposited protein is derived from:
robbins-ch20:systemic.e: Chronic inflammation (RA) causes reactive AA amyloidosis from the acute-phase protein SAA. AL amyloid from light chains is seen in plasma cell dyscrasias.

robbins-ch20:nephrosclerosis.q: 'Flea-bitten' kidney with onion-skin arteriolar thickening suggests:
robbins-ch20:nephrosclerosis.e: Malignant HT: petechiae on surface, hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis, fibrinoid necrosis.
Hyaline arteriolosclerosis → ischemic atrophy and small kidneys with a finely granular cortical surface.

robbins-ch20:nephrosclerosis.q: A 45-year-old man has headache and blurred vision. BP is 240/140 mm Hg, fundoscopy shows papilledema and creatinine has risen to 3.2 mg/dL with hematuria. Renal arterioles would most likely show:
robbins-ch20:nephrosclerosis.e: Malignant hypertension produces hyperplastic ('onion-skin') arteriolosclerosis with fibrinoid necrosis. Hyaline arteriolosclerosis is benign nephrosclerosis.

robbins-ch20:tma.q: A child develops bloody diarrhea, then hemolytic anemia with schistocytes, thrombocytopenia and AKI. The likely cause is:
TTP is caused by deficiency of:
robbins-ch20:tma.e: ADAMTS13 cleaves vWF multimers; deficiency (usually autoantibody) → platelet microthrombi.

robbins-ch20:tma.q: Fibromuscular dysplasia of the renal artery typically affects:
robbins-ch20:tma.e: Renal artery stenosis: atherosclerosis in older men; FMD in young women, with a 'string of beads' appearance on angiography.

robbins-ch20:tma.q: A 4-year-old girl has bloody diarrhea after visiting a petting zoo. A week later she has pallor, petechiae and oliguria; smear shows schistocytes, platelets 40,000/µL and creatinine 2.8 mg/dL. The primary mechanism of her renal injury is:
robbins-ch20:tma.e: Shiga toxin from STEC damages glomerular endothelium, triggering microthrombi (typical HUS). ADAMTS13 autoantibodies cause TTP; factor H mutations cause atypical HUS.

robbins-ch20:congenital.q: Horseshoe kidney most commonly involves fusion of:
robbins-ch20:congenital.e: ~90% fused at lower poles, 10% at upper poles.
No urine → oligohydramnios → Potter sequence (pulmonary hypoplasia); incompatible with life.

robbins-ch20:congenital.q: A 30-year-old woman has an incidental CT finding of two kidneys joined at their lower poles, lying lower than normal in the abdomen. During embryonic ascent, this fused kidney was trapped beneath the:
robbins-ch20:congenital.e: Horseshoe kidney (usually lower-pole fusion) is caught under the IMA during ascent. It is usually asymptomatic but predisposes to obstruction, stones and infection.

robbins-ch21:ureter.q: The most common cause of hydronephrosis in infants and children is:
robbins-ch21:ureter.e: Robbins: UPJ obstruction is the most common cause of hydronephrosis in infants and children.

robbins-ch21:ureter.q: Primary malignant tumors of the ureter are most often:
robbins-ch21:ureter.e: Ureteral tumors resemble those of the pelvis and bladder — mostly urothelial carcinomas, often multifocal.

robbins-ch21:ureter.q: A 2-month-old boy had unilateral left hydronephrosis on prenatal ultrasound. Postnatal imaging shows a dilated left renal pelvis with a normal-caliber ureter and a normal bladder; voiding cystourethrogram is normal. The most likely diagnosis is:
robbins-ch21:ureter.e: A dilated pelvis with a normal ureter localizes the block to the ureteropelvic junction, the most common cause of hydronephrosis in children. Valves cause bilateral hydronephrosis with an abnormal bladder.

robbins-ch21:ureterobs.q: Sclerosing retroperitoneal fibrosis is in a subset of patients related to:
robbins-ch21:ureterobs.e: Elevated IgG4 and IgG4-positive plasma cells; also drugs (ergot, β-blockers), inflammation, malignancy, or idiopathic (Ormond).

robbins-ch21:ureterobs.q: Bilateral hydronephrosis most often arises from:
robbins-ch21:ureterobs.e: Unilateral = proximal causes; bilateral = distal causes such as nodular prostatic hyperplasia.

robbins-ch21:ureterobs.q: A 58-year-old man with prior autoimmune pancreatitis has low back pain and creatinine 2.4 mg/dL. CT shows a periaortic soft-tissue mass encasing both ureters with bilateral hydronephrosis; serum IgG4 is high. Biopsy of the mass would most likely show:
o: Storiform fibrosis with IgG4 plasma cells
robbins-ch21:ureterobs.e: IgG4-related retroperitoneal fibrosis shows storiform fibrosis, obliterative phlebitis and many IgG4-positive plasma cells. Michaelis–Gutmann bodies define malakoplakia.

robbins-ch21:bladdercong.q: Bladder exstrophy predisposes to which carcinoma?
robbins-ch21:bladdercong.e: Exposed mucosa undergoes colonic glandular metaplasia → adenocarcinoma.

robbins-ch21:bladdercong.q: Carcinoma arising in a bladder diverticulum tends to present at higher stage because:
o: The muscularis propria is thin or absent

robbins-ch21:bladdercong.q: A 2-week-old boy has clear fluid draining from his umbilicus that increases when he cries; the fluid has a high urea concentration. The most likely diagnosis is:
robbins-ch21:bladdercong.e: Urine at the umbilicus means a persistent allantois–urachus tract to the bladder dome. A vitelline duct fistula drains meconium, not urine.

robbins-ch21:metaplasia.q: Extensive keratinizing squamous metaplasia of the bladder from Schistosoma haematobium predisposes to:
robbins-ch21:metaplasia.e: Schistosomiasis → squamous metaplasia → dysplasia → SCC (70% of cancers in endemic areas are squamous).

robbins-ch21:metaplasia.q: Extensive intestinal metaplasia in cystitis glandularis is a precursor to:
robbins-ch21:metaplasia.e: Goblet cell (intestinal) metaplasia, when extensive and multifocal, can progress to adenocarcinoma.

robbins-ch21:metaplasia.q: A 52-year-old woman with chronic recurrent cystitis has small nodules on cystoscopy. Biopsy shows nests of urothelium in the lamina propria with central lumens lined by cuboidal and columnar cells, without atypia. The diagnosis is:
robbins-ch21:metaplasia.e: Brunn nests with central gland-like lumens are cystitis glandularis, a reactive change; extensive intestinal-type change is a risk for adenocarcinoma. CIS shows malignant cells in flat urothelium.

robbins-ch21:grading.q: Urothelial carcinoma in situ is characterized by:
o: Malignant cells in a flat urothelium
Benign cords of cells growing inward
A papillary mass with fibrovascular cores
robbins-ch21:grading.e: CIS: cytologically malignant cells within a flat urothelium, often dyscohesive; may show pagetoid spread; cells shed into urine (cytology).

robbins-ch21:grading.q: A papillary tumor with thickened urothelium but minimal atypia is classified as:
robbins-ch21:grading.e: Papillary urothelial neoplasm of low malignant potential.

robbins-ch21:grading.q: Which papillary tumor has the highest risk of invasion and death (~25%)?
robbins-ch21:grading.e: High-grade papillary UC: dyscohesive anaplastic cells, frequent mitoses.

robbins-ch21:grading.q: A 67-year-old man who smokes has microscopic hematuria and positive urine cytology. Cystoscopy shows velvety red patches; biopsy shows flat urothelium replaced by large, pleomorphic, hyperchromatic cells without invasion. The most appropriate treatment is:
robbins-ch21:grading.e: This is urothelial carcinoma in situ, a high-grade flat lesion that often progresses to invasion; intravesical BCG is standard first-line therapy. Surveillance alone undertreats it.

robbins-ch21:staging.q: A bladder tumor invading the inner half of the muscularis propria is stage:
robbins-ch21:staging.e: T2a = superficial (inner half) muscularis propria; T2b = outer half.

robbins-ch21:staging.q: The key prognostic and treatment distinction in bladder cancer is:
robbins-ch21:staging.e: Non-muscle-invasive (Ta, Tis, T1) is 70–80%; muscle-invasive needs cystectomy or radiation + chemotherapy.

robbins-ch21:staging.q: The most common presenting symptom of bladder cancer is:
robbins-ch21:staging.e: Painless hematuria; investigate with cystoscopy and urine cytology.

robbins-ch21:staging.q: A 70-year-old man has a bladder tumor resected. Pathology shows urothelial carcinoma invading through the muscularis propria into the perivesical fat, seen only microscopically, without nodal involvement. The pathologic T stage is:
robbins-ch21:staging.e: Microscopic invasion of perivesical tissue = pT3a (macroscopic = pT3b). pT2b is invasion of the outer half of the muscularis propria.

robbins-ch21:othertum.q: A child has a grape-like polypoid mass protruding into the bladder. Diagnosis:
robbins-ch21:othertum.e: Sarcoma botryoides: the most common bladder sarcoma in childhood.

robbins-ch21:othertum.q: Small-cell carcinoma of the bladder is strongly associated with loss of:

A 61-year-old man has hematuria and passes mucus in his urine. Cystoscopy shows a mass at the bladder dome; histology shows mucin-secreting glandular epithelium without urothelial carcinoma components. The most likely diagnosis is:
robbins-ch21:othertum.e: A glandular mucin-secreting tumor at the dome arises from urachal remnants. Urothelial carcinoma is far commoner overall but is not purely glandular.

robbins-ch21:urethra.q: A small, red, painful mass at the external urethral meatus of an older woman is most likely:
robbins-ch21:urethra.e: Inflamed granulation tissue covered by friable mucosa; excision is curative.

robbins-ch21:urethra.q: Carcinomas of the distal urethra are most often:
robbins-ch21:urethra.e: Proximal → urothelial; distal → squamous (HPV); adenocarcinoma infrequent, mostly in women.

robbins-ch21:urethra.q: A 24-year-old man has dysuria and a watery urethral discharge, followed 3 weeks later by conjunctivitis and a swollen knee. Gram stain of the discharge shows neutrophils but no organisms. The most likely triggering organism is:
robbins-ch21:urethra.e: Nongonococcal urethritis followed by conjunctivitis and arthritis is reactive arthritis, most often after C. trachomatis. Gonorrhea would show gram-negative intracellular diplococci.

harrison-ch319:ap-aki.q: FENa ≤1%, U/P creatinine ≥40 and hyaline casts suggest:
harrison-ch319:ap-aki.e: Table 319-1: intact tubules reabsorb Na avidly in prerenal states.

harrison-ch319:ap-aki.q: An elevated BUN/creatinine ratio in prerenal states occurs because:
o: GFR rises and clears creatinine faster
Urea is reabsorbed but creatinine is not
harrison-ch319:ap-aki.e: Urea is reabsorbed along with water while creatinine is not, so urea clearance < creatinine clearance when tubular water reabsorption increases.

harrison-ch319:ap-aki.q: A 78-year-old woman has had vomiting for 3 days. BP is 92/58 mm Hg with dry mucous membranes; BUN is 64 mg/dL, creatinine 2.0 mg/dL, urine sodium 9 mEq/L and the sediment is bland. The most appropriate next step is:
harrison-ch319:ap-aki.e: BUN:Cr > 20, low urine Na and a bland sediment indicate prerenal azotemia from volume loss; restoring perfusion with isotonic fluid reverses it. Diuretics would worsen hypovolemia.

harrison-ch319:ap-syn.q: Nephrotic syndrome with which glomerular disease is most often associated with renal vein thrombosis?
harrison-ch319:ap-syn.e: Harrison: MN in nephrotic syndrome is most often associated with RVT.

harrison-ch319:ap-syn.q: A child with nephrotic syndrome and albumin <2 g/dL develops severe abdominal pain mimicking a surgical abdomen. This is called:

A 35-year-old man has cola-colored urine and ankle swelling. BP is 162/100 mm Hg; urinalysis shows dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts, protein excretion is 1.2 g/day and creatinine has risen to 2.1 mg/dL. His presentation is best classified as:
harrison-ch319:ap-syn.e: Hematuria with RBC casts, hypertension, sub-nephrotic proteinuria and falling GFR define the nephritic pattern. Nephrotic syndrome requires > 3.5 g/day proteinuria with hypoalbuminemia.

harrison-ch319:ap-hem.q: A 55-year-old has new microscopic hematuria without proteinuria or casts. The next step is:
o: Start an ACE inhibitor and recheck
harrison-ch319:ap-hem.e: New hematuria in the 4th decade or later warrants urologic evaluation and cystoscopy.

harrison-ch319:ap-hem.q: Hematuria after strenuous exercise should be:
harrison-ch319:ap-hem.e: Exercise-induced hematuria resolves; retest after rest.

harrison-ch319:ap-hem.q: A 22-year-old soldier collapses with muscle pain after a long march in the heat. His urine is tea-colored; dipstick is 3+ for blood but microscopy shows 0–2 RBCs/hpf. The dipstick result is best explained by:
harrison-ch319:ap-hem.e: The heme dipstick detects myoglobin (and hemoglobin) as well as RBCs; heme-positive urine without RBCs after exertional muscle injury indicates myoglobinuria from rhabdomyolysis.

o: NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb
harrison-ch320:cb-seg.e: TAL reabsorbs ~25% of filtered Na via NKCC2.

harrison-ch320:cb-seg.q: Vasopressin increases water permeability of the collecting duct by inserting:
harrison-ch320:cb-seg.e: V2 receptor → cAMP → AQP2 to the apical membrane.

harrison-ch320:cb-seg.q: A 58-year-old woman with hypertension has recurrent calcium stones and hypercalciuria. She is started on a drug that lowers BP and reduces urinary calcium excretion. Its molecular target is:
o: NCC in the distal convoluted tubule
Carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule
NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb
harrison-ch320:cb-seg.e: Thiazides block NCC in the DCT and increase calcium reabsorption, lowering urinary calcium. Loop diuretics (NKCC2) do the opposite and increase calcium excretion.

harrison-ch320:cb-inh.q: Hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with hypomagnesemia and low urinary calcium suggests:
Hypertension with hypokalemia and suppressed renin and aldosterone, responsive to amiloride:
Hypertension with hyperkalemia and acidosis responsive to thiazide:
harrison-ch320:cb-inh.e: Gordon syndrome (PHA-2): WNK/KLHL3/CUL3 mutations increase NCC activity.
