harrison-ch320:cb-inh.q: An 8-year-old boy has polyuria, growth delay and normal BP. Labs show K⁺ 2.6 mEq/L, HCO₃⁻ 32 mEq/L, high renin and aldosterone, high urinary calcium and nephrocalcinosis on ultrasound. The most likely defective transporter is:
o: NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb
NCC in the distal convoluted tubule
harrison-ch320:cb-inh.e: Bartter syndrome mimics loop diuretics: hypokalemic alkalosis with hypercalciuria. Gitelman (NCC) gives hypocalciuria and hypomagnesemia; ENaC gain (Liddle) causes hypertension with low renin.

harrison-ch320:cb-na.e: Disorders of Na⁺ concentration are disorders of water; ECF volume reflects total body Na⁺.

harrison-ch320:cb-na.q: ECF volume is determined mainly by:
harrison-ch320:cb-na.e: Regulated by RAAS, sympathetic activity, natriuretic peptides.

harrison-ch320:cb-na.q: A 70-year-old man with small cell lung cancer has confusion. He is euvolemic; serum Na⁺ is 122 mEq/L, serum osmolality 255 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 480 mOsm/kg and urine Na⁺ 50 mEq/L. His hyponatremia mainly reflects:
o: Sodium loss from the GI tract
Renal salt wasting from low aldosterone
harrison-ch320:cb-na.e: SIADH: ADH-driven water retention dilutes plasma Na⁺ in a euvolemic patient with inappropriately concentrated urine. Primary polydipsia would give maximally dilute urine (< 100 mOsm/kg).

harrison-ch321:aki-cause.q: The most common form of AKI is:
harrison-ch321:aki-cause.e: Harrison: prerenal azotemia is the most common form.

harrison-ch321:aki-cause.q: Why can NSAIDs precipitate AKI in a patient with heart failure?
o: They precipitate as crystals in tubules
They cause direct toxic tubular necrosis
They block angiotensin II efferent constriction
harrison-ch321:aki-cause.e: Autoregulation in low perfusion depends on afferent PG-mediated dilation and efferent Ang II constriction.
SCr rises in 1–2 days, peaks 3–5 days, recovers by ~7 days.

harrison-ch321:aki-cause.q: A 68-year-old smoker with refractory hypertension and an abdominal bruit is started on lisinopril. Within a week his creatinine rises from 1.3 to 2.5 mg/dL; urine sediment is bland. The mechanism of his AKI is:
harrison-ch321:aki-cause.e: With bilateral renal artery stenosis, GFR depends on angiotensin II constricting the efferent arteriole; an ACE inhibitor removes it and GFR falls. Afferent constriction is the NSAID/calcineurin mechanism.

harrison-ch321:aki-mx.q: Which is an indication for urgent dialysis in AKI?
harrison-ch321:aki-mx.e: Refractory volume overload, hyperkalemia, acidosis, some toxins, uremic complications (pericarditis, encephalopathy, bleeding).

harrison-ch321:aki-mx.q: AKI from scleroderma renal crisis should be treated with:

harrison-ch321:aki-mx.e: May need up to 10 L/day of fluid.

harrison-ch321:aki-mx.q: A 66-year-old man with oliguric AKI has K⁺ 7.1 mEq/L. ECG shows peaked T waves and a widened QRS. The first drug to give, and its effect, is:
o: Patiromer: binds K⁺ in the colon
IV insulin: shifts K⁺ into the cells
harrison-ch321:aki-mx.e: With ECG changes, IV calcium is given first to stabilize the myocardium within minutes; it does not lower K⁺. Insulin with glucose follows to shift K⁺ intracellularly.

harrison-ch322:ckd-stage.q: eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73m² with ACR 150 mg/g is classified as:
In the KDIGO heat map, risk of CKD progression increases with:
o: Falling GFR only; albuminuria adds no risk
Rising albuminuria only; GFR adds no risk
harrison-ch322:ckd-stage.e: Both axes independently increase mortality, CV death and progression.

harrison-ch322:ckd-stage.q: A 60-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has an eGFR of 52 mL/min/1.73 m² on two measurements 4 months apart and a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio of 420 mg/g. Her CKD category is:
harrison-ch322:ckd-stage.e: eGFR 45–59 = G3a; ACR > 300 mg/g = A3 (severely increased). A2 is 30–300 mg/g.

harrison-ch322:ckd-lyte.q: Hyperkalemia out of proportion to GFR in a diabetic with CKD suggests:
harrison-ch322:ckd-lyte.e: Type 4 RTA pattern in diabetes, obstruction, sickle cell nephropathy.

harrison-ch322:ckd-lyte.q: Metabolic acidosis in early CKD is usually non–anion gap because:
harrison-ch322:ckd-lyte.e: Reduced ammoniagenesis limits acid excretion; anion-gap acidosis appears as GFR falls further.

harrison-ch322:ckd-lyte.q: A 62-year-old man with diabetic CKD (eGFR 45) has K⁺ 5.9 mEq/L and a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. Plasma renin and aldosterone are both low, and urine pH is 5.2. The most likely disorder is:
harrison-ch322:ckd-lyte.e: Hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism in diabetic CKD causes type 4 RTA: hyperkalemia with NAGMA and preserved ability to acidify urine. Type 1 RTA has urine pH > 5.5 and usually hypokalemia.

harrison-ch322:ckd-slow.q: SGLT2 inhibitors reduce intraglomerular pressure by:
harrison-ch322:ckd-slow.e: More NaCl reaches the macula densa → tubuloglomerular feedback → afferent vasoconstriction.

harrison-ch322:ckd-slow.q: Combining an ACE inhibitor with an ARB in CKD:
harrison-ch322:ckd-slow.e: Dual RAS blockade increases harm (more AKI and cardiac events).

harrison-ch322:ckd-slow.q: Target BP in proteinuric CKD per Harrison:
A 56-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73 m² and ACR 600 mg/g despite maximal-dose losartan; BP is 128/78 mm Hg. The best addition to slow CKD progression is:
harrison-ch322:ckd-slow.e: SGLT2 inhibitors restore tubuloglomerular feedback (afferent constriction), lowering intraglomerular pressure and slowing CKD. Adding an ACE inhibitor to an ARB raises hyperkalemia and AKI risk without benefit.

harrison-ch323:hd.q: The principal mechanism of solute removal in hemodialysis is:
harrison-ch323:hd.e: Diffusion across a semipermeable membrane, down concentration gradients; ultrafiltration removes water.

harrison-ch323:hd.q: The vascular access with the longest patency and lowest infection rate:
The leading cause of ESKD in the United States:
harrison-ch323:hd.e: Diabetes accounts for ~45% of new ESKD cases (Harrison Ch 323).

harrison-ch323:hd.q: A 58-year-old man on thrice-weekly hemodialysis gains 3 kg of fluid between sessions. Removal of this excess fluid during treatment occurs mainly by:
harrison-ch323:hd.e: Fluid is removed by ultrafiltration, driven by a transmembrane hydrostatic pressure gradient; solutes like urea are removed by diffusion. Dextrose-driven osmotic ultrafiltration is how peritoneal dialysis removes fluid.

harrison-ch323:hdcx.q: The most common acute complication of hemodialysis:
harrison-ch323:hdcx.e: Especially in diabetics; manage by stopping UF and giving saline.

harrison-ch323:hdcx.q: Ultrafiltration rates above which value are associated with cardiovascular death?
A 19-year-old with newly diagnosed ESKD and BUN 180 mg/dL develops headache, vomiting and a seizure near the end of his first, long hemodialysis session. The mechanism is:
o: Cerebral edema from rapid urea removal
Air embolism through the venous line
harrison-ch323:hdcx.e: Dialysis disequilibrium: rapid lowering of plasma urea leaves brain osmolality higher, drawing water into the brain. It is prevented by short, gentle initial sessions.

harrison-ch323:pd.q: Peritonitis in a PD patient is defined by effluent WBC ≥100/mm³ with at least:
harrison-ch323:pd.e: Lower thresholds than SBP because of dextrose.

harrison-ch323:pd.q: Icodextrin in PD is used for:
harrison-ch323:pd.e: Used as last fill in CCPD or longest dwell in CAPD.

harrison-ch323:pd.q: A 52-year-old woman on peritoneal dialysis has abdominal pain and cloudy effluent. Effluent WBC count is 450/mm³ with 85% neutrophils; there is no exit-site discharge. The most likely organism is:
harrison-ch323:pd.e: PD peritonitis is most often from skin flora (coagulase-negative staphylococci) introduced at exchanges. Gram-negative or fungal peritonitis is less common and suggests bowel source or prior antibiotics.

harrison-ch324:ivn.q: An AV fistula that is hyperpulsatile and does not soften in diastole suggests:
harrison-ch324:ivn.e: Outflow stenosis increases pulsatility; inflow stenosis gives a weak 'empty' access.

harrison-ch324:ivn.q: An access with excessively high flow can be treated by:
harrison-ch324:ivn.e: Banding creates a controlled inflow stenosis.

harrison-ch324:ivn.q: A 60-year-old man on hemodialysis via a left arm AV fistula has progressive swelling of the entire left arm, with dilated veins over the chest wall. Fistula pressures are high during dialysis. The most likely cause is:
harrison-ch324:ivn.e: Whole-arm edema with chest wall collaterals means venous outflow is blocked centrally, often after prior central catheters. Steal causes hand pain and pallor, not swelling.

harrison-ch325:tx-imm.e: Prevented by ABO matching and crossmatch.

harrison-ch325:tx-imm.q: C4d staining in peritubular capillaries indicates:
harrison-ch325:tx-imm.e: Footprint of complement activation by donor-specific antibodies.

harrison-ch325:tx-imm.q: CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells respond primarily to donor:
harrison-ch325:tx-imm.e: CD4 → class II; CD8 → class I.

harrison-ch325:tx-imm.q: A 45-year-old man has a rising creatinine 3 months after a deceased-donor kidney transplant. Biopsy shows interstitial lymphocytes invading tubular epithelium (tubulitis); C4d staining is negative and donor-specific antibodies are absent. The diagnosis is:
harrison-ch325:tx-imm.e: Tubulitis with interstitial lymphocytes and no C4d/DSA is acute cellular rejection, driven by T cells recognizing donor HLA. C4d-positive capillaritis indicates antibody-mediated rejection.

harrison-ch325:tx-drug.q: Gingival hyperplasia and hirsutism are typical of:

o: Blocking the IL-2 receptor α chain
harrison-ch325:tx-drug.e: Costimulation blockade: binds CD80/CD86 on APCs, preventing CD28 costimulation.

harrison-ch325:tx-drug.q: A 52-year-old woman on a three-drug regimen after kidney transplant develops tremor, new-onset diabetes, hyperkalemia and hypertension. Trough level of one drug is high. That drug acts by:
o: Blocking CD80/86 binding to T-cell CD28
harrison-ch325:tx-drug.e: Tremor, diabetes, hyperkalemia and hypertension are classic tacrolimus toxicity; it binds FKBP-12 and inhibits calcineurin, blocking IL-2 gene transcription. mTOR inhibitors act downstream of the IL-2 receptor.

harrison-ch325:tx-inf.q: Cytomegalovirus and Pneumocystis infections after kidney transplant peak at:
The most common malignancies after kidney transplantation are:
Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease is most often associated with:

Ten weeks after a kidney transplant, a 50-year-old man (donor CMV-positive, recipient CMV-negative) has fever, leukopenia and elevated transaminases. Blood PCR shows a high viral load. The best treatment is:
harrison-ch325:tx-inf.e: CMV disease peaks 1–6 months after transplant, especially D+/R−; ganciclovir or valganciclovir is the treatment. Acyclovir has poor CMV activity.

harrison-ch326:gd-prot.q: Microalbuminuria is defined as albumin excretion of:
In normal urine, albumin accounts for what fraction of total urinary protein?
harrison-ch326:gd-prot.e: Normal urine (total protein < 150 mg/day) is mostly tubular uromodulin (Tamm–Horsfall) and filtered low-molecular-weight proteins; albumin is a minority (~20–60%). In glomerular proteinuria albumin becomes the dominant protein.

harrison-ch326:gd-prot.q: A 45-year-old man with type 1 diabetes has a urine dipstick negative for protein, but a spot urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio of 120 mg/g on two occasions. This finding is classified as:
harrison-ch326:gd-prot.e: ACR 30–300 mg/g (formerly microalbuminuria) is moderately increased albuminuria (A2), often below dipstick sensitivity. It is the earliest clinical sign of diabetic kidney disease.

harrison-ch326:gd-pat.e: With anti-GBM disease, thin BM disease, nail-patella.

harrison-ch326:gd-pat.q: A 65-year-old man with a prosthetic valve has 4 weeks of fever; blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. He develops hematuria with RBC casts, low C3 and creatinine 2.3 mg/dL. The kidney lesion is most likely:
harrison-ch326:gd-pat.e: Endocarditis causes an infection-associated nephritic syndrome with low complement from circulating immune complexes. Anti-GBM disease has normal complement and linear IgG.

harrison-ch326:gd-tx.q: First-line treatment of minimal change disease:
harrison-ch326:gd-tx.e: Steroid; other agents for relapses or resistance.

harrison-ch326:gd-tx.q: Pulmonary hemorrhage in anti-GBM disease responds to:

harrison-ch326:gd-tx.e: Reduces proteinuria in IgAN at risk of progression.

harrison-ch326:gd-tx.q: A 50-year-old man has chronic sinusitis, lung nodules, RBC casts and creatinine 3.2 mg/dL. PR3-ANCA is positive and biopsy shows pauci-immune crescentic GN. The most appropriate induction therapy is:
harrison-ch326:gd-tx.e: ANCA-associated GN is induced with glucocorticoids plus rituximab or cyclophosphamide. Budesonide is for IgA nephropathy and eculizumab for atypical HUS.

harrison-ch327:pkd-ad.q: ADPKD is caused by mutations in PKD1 in about what proportion of cases?
The most common extrarenal manifestation of ADPKD:
harrison-ch327:pkd-ad.e: Liver cysts; aneurysms 4–5× more frequent than general population.
V2 antagonist: lowers cAMP, which drives cyst growth.

harrison-ch327:pkd-ad.q: A 38-year-old woman with ADPKD has eGFR 70 mL/min/1.73 m² and rapidly enlarging kidneys on MRI. She starts a drug that slows cyst growth by lowering cAMP in collecting duct cells. Which monitoring is most important?
harrison-ch327:pkd-ad.e: Tolvaptan (V2 antagonist) can cause serious liver injury, so liver enzymes are checked regularly; its other main effect is aquaresis with thirst and polyuria.

harrison-ch327:pkd-ar.q: ARPKD is caused by mutations in:
The liver lesion in ARPKD is:

A newborn has respiratory distress, flattened facies and massively enlarged echogenic kidneys; pregnancy was complicated by oligohydramnios and both parents are healthy. The renal cysts in this disorder arise mainly from the:
harrison-ch327:pkd-ar.e: ARPKD (PKHD1) causes radially arranged fusiform dilation of collecting ducts throughout the cortex and medulla; survivors develop congenital hepatic fibrosis.

harrison-ch327:pkd-oth.q: Renal cysts with multifocal clear cell RCC, cerebellar hemangioblastoma and pheochromocytoma:
CKD with gout and few cysts in a family with UMOD mutation:

A 12-year-old girl has polyuria, polydipsia, growth failure and anemia; creatinine is 2.6 mg/dL with bland urine. Ultrasound shows normal-sized echogenic kidneys with small corticomedullary cysts, and she has retinal degeneration. The likely diagnosis is:
harrison-ch327:pkd-oth.e: Nephronophthisis is an autosomal recessive ciliopathy with a salt-wasting, concentrating defect, small corticomedullary cysts and ESKD in childhood (Senior–Løken with retinal disease). Medullary sponge kidney is benign with normal function.

harrison-ch328:tin-ain.q: The classic triad of drug-induced AIN (fever, rash, eosinophilia) is:
o: The exception rather than the rule
harrison-ch328:tin-ain.e: Harrison: most patients lack the full triad.

harrison-ch328:tin-ain.q: First step in suspected drug-induced AIN:
harrison-ch328:tin-ain.e: Then steroids if no improvement in ~1 week or rapid progression.

harrison-ch328:tin-ain.q: A 68-year-old woman develops AKI 3 weeks after starting nafcillin. Biopsy shows interstitial edema with lymphocytes and eosinophils. The drug was stopped, but after 7 days her creatinine is still rising. The next best step is:
harrison-ch328:tin-ain.e: If biopsy-proven drug-induced AIN does not improve after withdrawal, glucocorticoids may hasten recovery. Re-exposure is contraindicated, and there is no dialysis indication.

harrison-ch328:tin-imm.q: Sjögren syndrome renal involvement typically causes:
harrison-ch328:tin-imm.e: Most common renal manifestation; may also cause nephrogenic DI.

harrison-ch328:tin-imm.q: TIN with uveitis (TINU) is treated with:
harrison-ch328:tin-imm.e: Absolute indication for steroids in adults.

harrison-ch328:tin-imm.q: A 40-year-old woman has bilateral hilar adenopathy, calcium 11.8 mg/dL and creatinine 2.2 mg/dL with sterile pyuria. A kidney biopsy would most likely show:
harrison-ch328:tin-imm.e: Sarcoidosis causes granulomatous interstitial nephritis and hypercalcemia from macrophage 1α-hydroxylase. Lymphocytic TIN without granulomas is typical of Sjögren syndrome.

harrison-ch328:tin-chronic.q: Herbal weight-loss preparations causing interstitial fibrosis and urothelial carcinoma contain:
harrison-ch328:tin-chronic.e: Aristolochic acid nephropathy (Chinese herbal / Balkan nephropathy).

harrison-ch328:tin-chronic.q: Chronic lithium therapy most characteristically causes:
Which is NOT a major cause of papillary necrosis?

A 50-year-old man with bipolar disorder has taken lithium at therapeutic levels for 20 years. He passes 5 L of urine daily; urine osmolality is 150 mOsm/kg and does not rise after desmopressin. The mechanism is:
o: Deficient ADH release from the pituitary
harrison-ch328:tin-chronic.e: Lithium enters principal cells via ENaC and down-regulates AQP2, causing nephrogenic DI. Central DI would respond to desmopressin.

harrison-ch329:tma-types.q: TTP is defined by MAHA with ADAMTS13 activity below:

A 35-year-old woman has fever, confusion and petechiae. Hemoglobin is 7.8 g/dL with schistocytes, platelets 18,000/µL, LDH high and creatinine 1.6 mg/dL. ADAMTS13 activity is < 5%. The most appropriate treatment is:
harrison-ch329:tma-types.e: Acquired TTP (anti-ADAMTS13) is treated with urgent plasma exchange plus glucocorticoids (± caplacizumab). Eculizumab is for complement-mediated (atypical) HUS.

harrison-ch329:tma-ssc.e: AKI with abrupt hypertension and a bland sediment. Treat with ACE inhibitors.

harrison-ch329:tma-ssc.q: Scleroderma renal crisis occurs in what proportion of diffuse systemic sclerosis?

A 45-year-old woman with rapidly progressive diffuse skin thickening, recently started on high-dose prednisone, has BP 210/120 mm Hg, schistocytes and rising creatinine. The autoantibody most associated with this complication is:
harrison-ch329:tma-ssc.e: Scleroderma renal crisis is associated with early diffuse disease, anti-RNA polymerase III and high-dose glucocorticoids. Anticentromere marks limited disease with low renal-crisis risk.

harrison-ch330:st-type.q: Uric acid stones form when urine pH is consistently:
Staghorn calculi in a patient with recurrent Proteus UTIs are composed of:
harrison-ch330:st-type.e: Struvite = magnesium ammonium phosphate. Urease raises urine pH >8.

harrison-ch330:st-type.q: A 55-year-old man with gout has renal colic. The stone is not visible on plain x-ray but is seen on CT; urine pH is 5.0 on repeated samples. The best long-term therapy to dissolve and prevent these stones is:
harrison-ch330:st-type.e: Radiolucent stones in persistently acidic urine are uric acid; alkalinizing urine with potassium citrate dissolves and prevents them. Thiazides target hypercalciuric calcium stones.

harrison-ch330:st-risk.q: Higher dietary calcium intake is associated with:
o: Lower risk of calcium oxalate stones
Higher risk of calcium oxalate stones
harrison-ch330:st-risk.e: Dietary calcium binds oxalate in the gut; supplements may differ.

harrison-ch330:st-risk.q: Recommended urine volume for stone prevention:

A 40-year-old man with recurrent calcium oxalate stones follows a strict low-calcium diet. His 24-hour urine shows volume 1.1 L, high oxalate and normal calcium. The most appropriate dietary advice is:
harrison-ch330:st-risk.e: Dietary calcium binds oxalate in the gut, so a low-calcium diet raises oxalate absorption and stone risk; also aim for ≥ 2 L/day urine. Vitamin C is metabolized to oxalate.

harrison-ch330:st-mx.q: The imaging of choice for suspected renal colic:
In cystinuria, urine is alkalinized with potassium citrate rather than sodium salts because:
A drug that can increase spontaneous passage of a ureteral stone:
A 50-year-old woman has left flank pain, fever of 39.4 °C and BP 88/56 mm Hg. CT shows an 8-mm obstructing proximal ureteral stone with hydronephrosis. After starting antibiotics, the next step is:
harrison-ch330:st-mx.e: An infected obstructed kidney is a urologic emergency requiring prompt decompression; definitive stone treatment is deferred. Medical expulsive therapy is only for uncomplicated small stones.

harrison-ch331:uo-cause.q: The most common cause of bilateral hydronephrosis in boys:
Obstruction above the bladder typically produces:
harrison-ch331:uo-cause.e: Unilateral hydroureter/hydronephrosis. Lesions at or below the bladder cause bilateral involvement.

harrison-ch331:uo-cause.q: A 48-year-old woman has postcoital and intermenstrual bleeding, pelvic pain and creatinine 3.1 mg/dL. Ultrasound shows bilateral hydronephrosis with a normal bladder. The most likely cause of obstruction is:
harrison-ch331:uo-cause.e: Locally advanced cervical cancer invades the parametrium and compresses both ureters, a classic cause of bilateral hydronephrosis in women. Bilateral simultaneous stones are rare.

harrison-ch331:uo-phys.q: Partial bilateral urinary obstruction often causes:
harrison-ch331:uo-phys.e: Hyperkalemic distal RTA with salt wasting, plus acquired nephrogenic DI.

harrison-ch331:uo-phys.q: Acute partial bilateral obstruction can mimic:
harrison-ch331:uo-phys.e: High BUN/Cr, concentrated urine, Na retention.

harrison-ch331:uo-phys.q: A 72-year-old man with prostatic enlargement reports 3.5 L/day of urine and nocturia; ultrasound shows bilateral hydronephrosis. Urine osmolality is 240 mOsm/kg and does not rise after desmopressin. The polyuria is best explained by:
harrison-ch331:uo-phys.e: Partial obstruction damages tubules and down-regulates AQP2, causing an acquired nephrogenic DI-like concentrating defect. Central DI would respond to desmopressin.

harrison-ch331:uo-dx.q: Hydronephrosis may be absent on ultrasound despite obstruction when:
o: The bladder is distended and full
harrison-ch331:uo-dx.e: Very early obstruction (<48 h) or retroperitoneal fibrosis; also volume contraction, staghorn calculi, infiltrative disease.

harrison-ch331:uo-dx.q: After how long of complete obstruction is recovery of GFR unlikely?
harrison-ch331:uo-dx.e: Partial recovery after 1–2 weeks; unlikely after 8 weeks.

harrison-ch331:uo-dx.q: Postobstructive diuresis typically follows relief of:
harrison-ch331:uo-dx.e: Hypotonic urine rich in Na, K, PO₄, Mg.

harrison-ch331:uo-dx.q: A 76-year-old man has suprapubic pain and has not voided for 18 hours. The bladder is palpable to the umbilicus, creatinine is 3.8 mg/dL and ultrasound shows bilateral hydronephrosis. The best initial step is:
harrison-ch331:uo-dx.e: Bladder outlet obstruction is relieved first with a urethral (or suprapubic) catheter; watch for postobstructive diuresis afterward. Nephrostomies are for obstruction above the bladder.

pharm-renal:sglt2.e: Block glucose and Na⁺ reabsorption → glucosuria and mild natriuresis.

pharm-renal:sglt2.q: SGLT2 inhibitors protect the kidney in CKD mainly by:
pharm-renal:sglt2.e: More Na⁺ at the macula densa → afferent constriction → ↓ intraglomerular pressure; an initial small eGFR dip is expected.

pharm-renal:sglt2.q: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 8.1%), eGFR 55 mL/min/1.73 m² and albuminuria starts a new oral drug. Two weeks later urine dipstick shows 3+ glucose with a plasma glucose of 130 mg/dL, and he develops a genital yeast infection. The drug acts by inhibiting which transporter?
o: Na⁺–glucose cotransporter in the early PT
Na⁺–Cl⁻ cotransporter in the early DCT
Epithelial Na⁺ channel in collecting duct
pharm-renal:sglt2.e: Glucosuria at normal plasma glucose plus mycotic genital infection points to an SGLT2 inhibitor (e.g., empagliflozin) blocking proximal Na⁺–glucose reabsorption; NKCC2 is the loop diuretic target.

pharm-renal:adh.e: V₂ antagonist for euvolemic or hypervolemic hyponatremia (SIADH, HF); also slows ADPKD; hepatotoxic.

pharm-renal:adh.q: Desmopressin treats central DI by acting on:
o: NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb
V₂ receptors in the collecting duct
V₁ receptors on vascular smooth muscle
pharm-renal:adh.e: V₂ → AQP2 insertion. Nephrogenic DI does not respond; use thiazide and amiloride (for lithium).

pharm-renal:adh.q: A 62-year-old man with small cell lung cancer has confusion. He is euvolemic; serum Na⁺ 124 mEq/L, serum osmolality 258 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 480 mOsm/kg, urine Na⁺ 45 mEq/L. Fluid restriction fails. Which drug directly targets the cause of his hyponatremia?
pharm-renal:adh.e: Ectopic ADH (SIADH) is countered by the V₂ receptor antagonist tolvaptan; desmopressin is a V₂ agonist and would worsen it.

pharm-renal:resist.q: Diuretic resistance in heart failure can be overcome by adding:
pharm-renal:resist.e: Sequential nephron blockade: metolazone + loop; watch K⁺ and Na⁺.

pharm-renal:resist.q: A cause of loop diuretic resistance:
pharm-renal:resist.e: Hypertrophied distal tubule ↑ Na⁺ reabsorption; also NSAIDs, poor absorption (gut edema), low renal perfusion.

pharm-renal:resist.q: A 71-year-old woman with heart failure remains edematous despite IV furosemide 80 mg twice daily; urine output is low and spot urine Na⁺ is 25 mEq/L. Metolazone is added and diuresis improves. Metolazone works here by blocking:
o: ENaC in collecting duct principal cells
NCC in the hypertrophied distal tubule
NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb
pharm-renal:resist.e: Chronic loop diuretic use causes distal tubule hypertrophy with ↑ Na⁺ reabsorption; a thiazide-like drug blocks NCC there (sequential nephron blockade). NKCC2 is already blocked by furosemide.

pharm-renal:aki.q: Which drug combination raises AKI risk ('triple whammy')?
pharm-renal:aki.e: Afferent constriction, efferent dilation and volume depletion.
Proximal tubular injury; monitor levels and creatinine.

pharm-renal:aki.q: A 72-year-old man on lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide starts ibuprofen for knee osteoarthritis. After 3 days of diarrhea his creatinine rises from 1.0 to 2.6 mg/dL; urine sediment is bland and FENa is 0.5%. How does ibuprofen contribute to this injury?
o: Direct necrosis of proximal tubule cells
pharm-renal:aki.e: Prerenal AKI: NSAIDs remove prostaglandin afferent vasodilation while the ACE inhibitor removes efferent constriction ('triple whammy'). Loss of efferent tone is the ACE inhibitor's contribution, not the NSAID's.

pharm-renal:ckd.q: Drugs proven to slow proteinuric CKD:
pharm-renal:ckd.e: ± finerenone in diabetes; all lower intraglomerular pressure or fibrosis.

pharm-renal:ckd.q: After starting an ACE inhibitor, a creatinine rise up to about 30% is:
o: A sign of acute tubular necrosis
An indication to stop at once
pharm-renal:ckd.e: Reflects efferent dilation; stop if higher or K⁺ rises dangerously.

pharm-renal:ckd.q: A 55-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has BP 142/88 mm Hg, eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73 m² and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 600 mg/g. Lisinopril is started. Its main renoprotective mechanism is:
o: Afferent constriction lowering renal blood flow
Restoring nephrin in the podocyte slit diaphragm
pharm-renal:ckd.e: Blocking angiotensin II dilates the efferent arteriole, reducing intraglomerular pressure and albuminuria in diabetic nephropathy; it does not constrict the afferent arteriole.

pharm-renal:anemia.q: Before starting an ESA in CKD anemia, ensure:
pharm-renal:anemia.e: Check ferritin and TSAT; iron deficiency causes ESA hyporesponsiveness.

pharm-renal:anemia.q: Targeting a high hemoglobin (> 13 g/dL) with ESAs increases:

A 64-year-old man with CKD stage 4 (eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73 m²) has fatigue. Hb 8.9 g/dL, MCV 88 fL, low reticulocyte count, ferritin 650 ng/mL, transferrin saturation 38%; stool occult blood is negative. Most appropriate treatment?
pharm-renal:anemia.e: Normocytic hypoproliferative anemia of CKD reflects ↓ renal erythropoietin; with ferritin > 500 ng/mL and TSAT > 30% iron stores are replete, so an ESA is indicated. Iron is tried first only when ferritin ≤ 500 and TSAT ≤ 30%.

pharm-renal:mbd.q: Calcitriol is used in CKD because:
o: It blocks PTH receptors on bone
pharm-renal:mbd.e: Renal 1α-hydroxylase is lost; calcitriol raises calcium and suppresses PTH; can raise phosphate.
Avoids calcium loading and vascular calcification.

pharm-renal:mbd.q: A 60-year-old woman on hemodialysis has pruritus. Serum Ca²⁺ 9.8 mg/dL, phosphate 7.2 mg/dL, PTH 650 pg/mL; CT shows extensive coronary artery calcification. Dietary phosphate restriction has failed. Best drug to lower her phosphate?
pharm-renal:mbd.e: A non-calcium binder avoids adding calcium load to existing vascular calcification; calcitriol raises gut phosphate absorption and aluminum is toxic long term.

pharm-renal:hyperk.q: In hyperkalemia with ECG changes, the first drug is:
pharm-renal:hyperk.e: Stabilizes the cardiac membrane; does not lower K⁺.

pharm-renal:hyperk.q: Which drugs shift K⁺ into cells?
pharm-renal:hyperk.e: Insulin is given with glucose. Removal: diuretics, binders (patiromer, SZC), dialysis.

pharm-renal:hyperk.q: A 66-year-old man with end-stage renal disease missed two dialysis sessions and has muscle weakness. Serum K⁺ is 7.4 mEq/L and the ECG shows peaked T waves and a widened QRS. The first drug given acts by:
o: Increasing K⁺ secretion in collecting duct
Binding K⁺ in the colon for excretion
Shifting K⁺ into cells via Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase
pharm-renal:hyperk.e: IV calcium gluconate antagonizes the membrane effects of hyperkalemia within minutes but does not lower K⁺; insulin/β₂ agonists shift K⁺ in afterwards.

pharm-renal:sodium.q: Rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia risks:
pharm-renal:sodium.e: Limit correction to about 8–10 mEq/L in 24 h.

pharm-renal:sodium.q: Which diuretic class is a common cause of hyponatremia?
pharm-renal:sodium.e: Impair urinary dilution in the DCT.

pharm-renal:sodium.q: A 45-year-old woman with alcohol use disorder is admitted with serum Na⁺ 108 mEq/L; after hypertonic saline her Na⁺ is 126 mEq/L 24 hours later. Three days later she develops dysarthria, dysphagia and quadriparesis, and MRI shows a T2 lesion in the central pons. Most likely diagnosis?
pharm-renal:sodium.e: An 18 mEq/L rise in 24 h exceeds the safe limit (~8–10) and causes central pontine myelinolysis; Wernicke causes ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and confusion, not a pontine lesion.

pharm-renal:acidbase.e: Hyperchloremic acidosis from urinary HCO₃⁻ loss.
Contraction alkalosis plus ↑ distal H⁺ and K⁺ secretion.

pharm-renal:acidbase.q: A 28-year-old man takes a drug for altitude sickness prophylaxis before a trek. Labs: pH 7.32, HCO₃⁻ 17 mEq/L, PaCO₂ 32 mm Hg, Na⁺ 140 mEq/L, Cl⁻ 113 mEq/L; urine pH 7.5. His acid–base disturbance results from:
o: Proximal HCO₃⁻ wasting from CA inhibition
pharm-renal:acidbase.e: Acetazolamide blocks proximal carbonic anhydrase → urinary HCO₃⁻ loss and a normal anion gap (10) metabolic acidosis with alkaline urine; organic anions would raise the gap.

renal-physio-2:features.q: Which finding distinguishes Gitelman from Bartter syndrome?
renal-physio-2:features.e: Gitelman mimics a thiazide (↓ urine Ca²⁺, ↓ Mg²⁺); Bartter mimics a loop diuretic (↑ urine Ca²⁺).

renal-physio-2:features.q: Hypertension with hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis and LOW renin and aldosterone suggests:
renal-physio-2:features.e: Overactive ENaC (or SAME) drives Na⁺ retention without aldosterone.

renal-physio-2:features.q: A 25-year-old man has BP 168/104 mm Hg, K⁺ 2.9 mEq/L and HCO₃⁻ 31. Renin and aldosterone are both very low. His father had early hypertension. Which drug best treats the cause?
renal-physio-2:features.e: Liddle syndrome: ENaC gain of function; amiloride blocks ENaC, while spironolactone does not help because aldosterone is not the driver.

o: Macula densa cells of the distal tubule
JG cells of the afferent arteriole
Principal cells of the collecting duct
renal-physio-2:endofx.e: Triggered by ↓ renal perfusion pressure, ↓ NaCl at the macula densa and β₁ stimulation. JG = juxtaglomerular (modified smooth muscle) cells.
Released in response to hypoxia; falls in CKD → normocytic anemia.

renal-physio-2:endofx.q: A 70-year-old woman with heart failure on lisinopril starts ibuprofen for knee pain. A week later her creatinine has doubled. The main mechanism is:
o: Acute tubular necrosis from ibuprofen crystals
Increased Ang II tone at the efferent arteriole
Loss of afferent PG dilation plus efferent dilation
renal-physio-2:endofx.e: NSAIDs constrict the afferent and ACE inhibitors dilate the efferent, so glomerular pressure falls when renal perfusion is already low.

renal-physio-3:lytes.q: Peaked T waves and a widening QRS suggest:
renal-physio-3:lytes.e: Hypokalemia gives U waves and flattened T waves.

renal-physio-3:lytes.q: Hypokalemia that does not correct with potassium replacement should prompt correction of:
renal-physio-3:lytes.e: Low Mg²⁺ increases renal K⁺ wasting.

renal-physio-3:lytes.q: A patient with lung cancer has confusion, constipation, polyuria and kidney stones. Which ECG finding is expected?
renal-physio-3:lytes.e: Hypercalcemia (e.g., PTHrP) shortens the QT; hypocalcemia prolongs it.

renal-physio-3:rta.q: Which renal tubular acidosis causes hyperkalemia?
renal-physio-3:rta.e: Hypoaldosteronism or aldosterone resistance; types 1 and 2 cause hypokalemia.

o: Bicarbonate wasting in the proximal tubule
renal-physio-3:rta.e: α-intercalated cells cannot secrete H⁺; calcium phosphate stones are common.

renal-physio-3:rta.q: A 45-year-old woman with dry eyes and dry mouth has a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis, K⁺ 2.8 mEq/L, urine pH 6.5 and nephrocalcinosis. The most likely diagnosis is:
renal-physio-3:rta.e: Sjögren syndrome is a classic autoimmune cause of distal RTA.

renal-patho-1:casts.q: Muddy brown granular casts in the urine suggest:
renal-patho-1:casts.e: Sloughed tubular cells form granular casts.

renal-patho-1:casts.q: WBC casts are most consistent with:
renal-patho-1:casts.e: Casts form in tubules, so they localize inflammation to the kidney; cystitis gives pyuria without casts.

renal-patho-1:casts.q: A 7-year-old boy has periorbital edema. Urinalysis shows 4+ protein and oval fat bodies with a Maltese cross pattern under polarized light. Which glomerular finding is expected on electron microscopy?
renal-patho-1:casts.e: Fatty casts point to nephrotic syndrome; in a child that is usually minimal change disease.

renal-patho-2:incont.q: Leakage of urine when coughing or sneezing is:
renal-patho-2:incont.e: Raised intra-abdominal pressure overcomes a weak sphincter.

renal-patho-2:incont.q: A high postvoid residual volume suggests:
renal-patho-2:incont.e: Incomplete emptying, from detrusor underactivity or outlet obstruction.

renal-patho-2:incont.q: A 72-year-old man with long-standing diabetes and peripheral neuropathy has constant dribbling of urine and a palpable bladder. The most likely mechanism is:
o: Urethral hypermobility from weak pelvic floor
Detrusor overactivity from loss of inhibition
renal-patho-2:incont.e: Diabetic autonomic neuropathy causes an atonic bladder and overflow incontinence.

renal-patho-3:papnec.q: Which condition is a classic cause of renal papillary necrosis?
renal-patho-3:papnec.e: Also diabetes, acute pyelonephritis and analgesics (NSAIDs).

renal-patho-3:papnec.q: Diffuse cortical necrosis is classically associated with:
renal-patho-3:papnec.e: Vasospasm plus DIC infarcts both cortices.

renal-patho-3:papnec.q: A 24-year-old man with sickle cell trait has sudden gross hematuria and left flank pain after a week of daily ibuprofen and dehydration. CT urography shows a 'ring sign' at a calyx. The most likely diagnosis is:
renal-patho-3:papnec.e: Low oxygen tension in the medulla promotes sickling and papillary infarction; a sloughed papilla can obstruct.

renal-patho-2:ic.q: Interstitial cystitis typically presents with bladder pain that:
o: Comes with fever and pyuria on urinalysis
Worsens with filling, eases after voiding
Is typically accompanied by gross hematuria
Is relieved when the bladder is full
renal-patho-2:ic.e: Chronic bladder pain related to filling, with normal urinalysis and culture.

renal-patho-2:ic.q: A 34-year-old woman has 4 months of suprapubic pain and frequency. Urinalysis and urine culture are repeatedly normal. She also has fibromyalgia. The most likely diagnosis is:
renal-patho-2:ic.e: A diagnosis of exclusion; associated with other chronic pain syndromes. Also called bladder pain syndrome.

renal-physio-3:nawork.q: In a patient with hyponatremia, the first test to order is:
renal-physio-3:nawork.e: Serum osmolality separates hypertonic and isotonic (pseudo) hyponatremia from true hypotonic hyponatremia.

renal-physio-3:nawork.q: Glucose rises from 100 to 600 mg/dL. The measured Na⁺ falls by roughly:
renal-physio-3:nawork.e: About 1.6 mEq/L per 100 mg/dL rise in glucose: 5 × 1.6 = 8.

renal-physio-3:nawork.q: Correcting chronic hyponatremia faster than about 10–12 mEq/L in 24 hours (8 in high-risk patients) mainly risks:
renal-physio-3:nawork.e: Rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia can cause osmotic demyelination (central pontine myelinolysis).

renal-physio-3:nawork.q: A man with hypernatremia has a urine osmolality of 90 mOsm/kg that rises to 450 mOsm/kg after desmopressin. The diagnosis is:
renal-physio-3:nawork.e: Dilute urine that concentrates with desmopressin indicates lack of ADH (central DI).

nephron-pathway:tracker.q: Which nephron segment reabsorbs the largest fraction of filtered Mg²⁺?
nephron-pathway:tracker.e: About 60–70% of filtered Mg²⁺ is reabsorbed paracellularly in the TAL; the PCT takes only ~15–25%.

nephron-pathway:tracker.q: Which substance is normally both filtered and secreted by the proximal tubule, so its clearance exceeds GFR?
nephron-pathway:tracker.e: PAH is filtered and secreted by organic anion transporters; inulin is filtered only, glucose is fully reabsorbed.

nephron-pathway:tracker.q: In a research study, a healthy 25-year-old man receives a constant infusion of para-aminohippurate at a low plasma concentration. Its clearance is 625 mL/min, while inulin clearance is 120 mL/min. The PAH clearance best estimates his:
nephron-pathway:tracker.e: PAH is filtered and almost completely secreted, so its clearance ≈ effective renal plasma flow; GFR is the inulin value and RBF = RPF/(1 − Hct).

nephron-pathway:pt1.q: The early proximal tubule reabsorbs Na⁺ mainly together with:
nephron-pathway:pt1.e: Early PCT: Na⁺ cotransport with organic solutes and Na⁺/H⁺ exchange (HCO₃⁻ reclaim); Cl⁻ follows later.

nephron-pathway:pt1.q: Fluid leaving the proximal tubule, compared with plasma, is:
nephron-pathway:pt1.e: Water follows solute through AQP1, so ~65% of filtrate is reabsorbed isosmotically.

nephron-pathway:pt1.q: An 8-year-old boy has bowed legs and poor growth. Labs: plasma glucose 90 mg/dL with 2+ glucosuria, generalized aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, serum phosphate 2.1 mg/dL and serum HCO₃⁻ 16 mEq/L with normal anion gap. Which nephron segment is dysfunctional?
nephron-pathway:pt1.e: Fanconi syndrome: global loss of proximal Na⁺-coupled reabsorption (glucose, amino acids, phosphate, HCO₃⁻) causing hypophosphatemic rickets and type 2 RTA; distal segments do not handle these solutes.

nephron-pathway:tal.q: The thick ascending limb is called the diluting segment because it:
o: Secretes free water into the lumen
Reabsorbs NaCl but is impermeable to water
Responds to ADH by inserting AQP2
nephron-pathway:tal.e: NKCC2 moves NaCl out while water cannot follow, so tubular fluid becomes hypotonic.

nephron-pathway:tal.q: A drug that blocks NKCC2 in the TAL would increase urinary loss of:
nephron-pathway:tal.e: Loss of the lumen-positive voltage stops paracellular Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ reabsorption (loop diuretics).

nephron-pathway:dct.q: Ca²⁺ reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule is increased by:
nephron-pathway:dct.e: PTH acts on the DCT to increase transcellular Ca²⁺ reabsorption.

nephron-pathway:dct.q: The Na⁺ transporter in the apical membrane of the early DCT is:
nephron-pathway:dct.e: NCC is the target of thiazides; ENaC is in principal cells.

nephron-pathway:dct.q: A 22-year-old woman has recurrent muscle cramps. BP 108/68 mm Hg. Serum K⁺ 2.9 mEq/L, Mg²⁺ 1.2 mg/dL, HCO₃⁻ 31 mEq/L; urinary calcium is low. She takes no medications. A mutation most likely affects the:
nephron-pathway:dct.e: Gitelman syndrome mimics a thiazide: hypokalemic alkalosis, hypomagnesemia and hypocalciuria from loss of DCT NCC. Bartter (NKCC2) causes hypercalciuria instead.

nephron-pathway:pc.q: Aldosterone increases K⁺ secretion by principal cells mainly by:
nephron-pathway:pc.e: More Na⁺ entry makes the lumen negative and more K⁺ is pumped into the cell, driving K⁺ out through ROMK.

nephron-pathway:pc.q: Amiloride causes hyperkalemia because it blocks:
nephron-pathway:pc.e: Less Na⁺ entry reduces the lumen-negative potential that drives K⁺ secretion.

nephron-pathway:mcd.q: In the presence of ADH, the inner medullary collecting duct reabsorbs urea through:
nephron-pathway:mcd.e: ADH-stimulated urea recycling builds the medullary osmotic gradient.

nephron-pathway:mcd.q: A patient lacking ADH produces urine with an osmolality closest to:
nephron-pathway:mcd.e: Without ADH the collecting duct stays water-impermeable and dilute fluid from the TAL is excreted.

renal-micro:upath.q: Enterobacterales account for what share of urinary tract infections?
renal-micro:upath.e: Murray puts Enterobacterales behind more than 70% of UTIs, and a quarter to a third of bacteraemias.

renal-micro:upath.q: A 24-year-old sexually active woman has dysuria and frequency. Which organism is the most likely cause?
renal-micro:upath.e: UPEC is the dominant community uropathogen; S. saprophyticus is the usual second in this group.

renal-micro:upath.q: Which group of urinary isolates is linked to infection stones?
renal-micro:upath.e: The stone-formers share urease, which alkalinises urine and precipitates struvite and apatite.

renal-micro:entero-b.q: Which set of reactions fits the family Enterobacterales?
o: Ferments glucose, reduces nitrate, catalase +, oxidase −
Does not ferment glucose, catalase +, oxidase +
renal-micro:entero-b.e: Oxidase negativity is the quick test separating them from Pseudomonas and from Vibrio.

renal-micro:entero-b.q: Which adhesin is the main uropathogenic factor of E. coli?
renal-micro:entero-b.e: Dr fimbriae and AAF also bind bladder and upper-tract cells so the organism is not voided out.

renal-micro:entero-b.q: A urine culture grows a lactose-negative organism that swarms across the blood agar. Urease is positive and indole negative. The isolate is:
renal-micro:entero-b.e: Swarming plus urease identifies P. mirabilis, the classic organism behind struvite stones.

renal-micro:entero-b.q: Proteus urease raises urinary pH. What follows?
renal-micro:entero-b.e: Urea splits into CO2 and ammonia; the alkaline urine is also toxic to the uroepithelium.

renal-micro:entero-b.q: Mucoid colonies on MacConkey agar from a hospital urine specimen suggest:
renal-micro:entero-b.e: The prominent capsule gives wet, heaped colonies and raises virulence; Klebsiella is also non-motile.

renal-micro:gp-cocci.q: Which test separates Staphylococcus saprophyticus from S. epidermidis?
renal-micro:gp-cocci.e: S. saprophyticus is novobiocin resistant; S. epidermidis is susceptible. Both are catalase + and coagulase −.

renal-micro:gp-cocci.q: A urinary isolate is catalase negative, PYR positive, hydrolyses bile esculin and grows in 6.5% NaCl. It is:
renal-micro:gp-cocci.e: Growth in 6.5% NaCl separates enterococci from the non-enterococcal group D streptococci.

renal-micro:gp-cocci.q: Why do enterococci cause UTI mainly in patients hospitalised for long periods?
o: They spread between patients by respiratory droplets
They grow only at temperatures above 40 °C
They resist the cephalosporins used broadly there
They need a urinary catheter to survive at all
renal-micro:gp-cocci.e: Broad-spectrum therapy clears competing flora; adherence and biofilm formation do the rest.

renal-micro:gp-cocci.q: Coagulase-negative staphylococci infect prosthetic material mainly because they:
o: Release urease that alkalinises the urine
Carry a polysaccharide capsule rich in alginate
Produce a slime layer that sticks to foreign bodies
Secrete an exotoxin that kills neutrophils
renal-micro:gp-cocci.e: Slime anchors them to catheters, shunts and prosthetic valves and shields them from phagocytes and drugs.

renal-micro:nonferm.q: Which result set identifies Pseudomonas aeruginosa?
o: Catalase negative, PYR positive, bile esculin positive
renal-micro:nonferm.e: Acinetobacter is oxidase negative and non-motile, which is how Harr separates the two.

renal-micro:nonferm.q: Ceftazidime exposure can induce ampC expression in Pseudomonas. This is an example of:
renal-micro:nonferm.e: Biofilm on a catheter triggers the same adaptive response; intrinsic resistance is porin plus efflux.

renal-micro:nonferm.q: Which colony description fits P. aeruginosa?
o: Dry buff colonies appearing after six weeks
Mucoid pink colonies on MacConkey agar
Flat pink colonies ringed by bile precipitate
renal-micro:nonferm.e: Pyocyanin and pyoverdin give the colour; the isolate is usually beta-haemolytic.

renal-micro:fungi-myco.q: Candida is cultured from the urine of a catheterised diabetic patient with no symptoms. This most likely represents:
renal-micro:fungi-myco.e: Benign colonisation is the commonest finding in this setting, although cystitis and renal abscess can occur.

renal-micro:fungi-myco.q: Bladder colonisation with Candida is essentially not seen unless the patient has:
o: Recently travelled to an endemic area
A catheter, diabetes or urinary obstruction
renal-micro:fungi-myco.e: Without one of those, yeast in urine should prompt a second look at the specimen.

renal-micro:fungi-myco.q: Why is Mycobacterium tuberculosis harder to recover from urine than from sputum?
o: Mycobacteria will not grow on any solid culture medium
Urine kills mycobacteria within minutes of being voided
Organisms are fewer, so volume and repeat specimens matter
Urinary isolates lose the acid-fast cell wall
renal-micro:fungi-myco.e: Murray asks for repeat specimens and large volumes; the specimen table wants at least 10 mL for mycobacteria.

renal-micro:virulence.q: Why must a uropathogen adhere in order to establish infection?
o: Adherent bacteria avoid being seen on Gram stain
Normal bladder function flushes out organisms that are not attached
Attachment is required before bacteria can divide
Urine lacks the nutrients bacteria need unless they attach
renal-micro:virulence.e: Adhesins at the fimbrial tips act as lectins and bind sugars on the host cell surface.

renal-micro:virulence.q: P fimbriae bind which host receptor?
o: Tamm–Horsfall protein in the tubular lumen
Gal-Gal of the P blood group antigen
renal-micro:virulence.e: Most E. coli isolates that cause pyelonephritis carry P fimbriae.

renal-micro:virulence.q: Which pair are innate defences of the urinary tract?
renal-micro:virulence.e: Together with urine flow they remove organisms that cannot hold on.

renal-micro:biofilm.q: What has to happen before bacteria switch on biofilm production?
o: Oxygen tension in the urine falls to zero
An antibiotic is given at a sub-inhibitory dose
The host mounts an antibody response
Enough organisms accumulate to form a quorum
renal-micro:biofilm.e: In Pseudomonas, N-acyl homoserine lactone reaching a threshold turns on the polysaccharide genes.

renal-micro:biofilm.q: Why are catheter-associated infections hard to treat once a biofilm forms?
o: Biofilm bacteria lose their cell wall and no longer Gram stain
Antibiotics are destroyed by the catheter material
The polysaccharide web shields bacteria from host defences and antibiotics
renal-micro:biofilm.e: Biofilm on a catheter can also trigger adaptive resistance genes.

renal-micro:specimen.q: Why is the first portion of a voided or catheter specimen discarded?
o: It is contaminated by urethral flora
It is too dilute to culture
It has the lowest pH of the stream
It contains inhibitors of bacterial growth
renal-micro:specimen.e: Several bacterial species colonise the urethra, so the midstream portion is what goes to culture.

renal-micro:specimen.q: A urine specimen for culture cannot be plated immediately. What should be done?
o: Refrigerate it or use a bacteriostatic preservative
Add formalin to the container to stop overgrowth
Leave it at room temperature until the morning
Freeze it at −20 °C and thaw it before plating
renal-micro:specimen.e: Uropathogens multiply in urine at room temperature, which falsifies the colony count.

renal-micro:specimen.q: Which collection method is the only valid one for anaerobic urine culture?
renal-micro:specimen.e: It bypasses the urethra entirely and is collected into a sterile anaerobic tube or vial.

renal-micro:specimen.q: Murray's specimen table asks for what volume of urine when mycobacteria are sought?
renal-micro:specimen.e: Bacterial culture needs only 1 mL; the larger volume offsets the low organism burden.

renal-micro:culture.q: Why is a measured 1–10 µL loopful of urine plated rather than an arbitrary drop?
o: To dilute out any antibiotic in the specimen
To stop the agar plate from drying out
To spread the inoculum evenly over the agar
So organisms per millilitre can be calculated
renal-micro:culture.e: Quantitation is what makes an isolate interpretable; one selective and one non-selective medium are used.

renal-micro:culture.q: Under the 2019 IDSA definition, asymptomatic bacteriuria in a woman requires:
o: Two consecutive voided specimens with at least 10⁵ CFU/mL
A single specimen with at least 10² CFU/mL
A single voided specimen with at least 10⁵ CFU/mL
renal-micro:culture.e: Men need only one specimen; the two specimens for women should be within about two weeks.

renal-micro:culture.q: How does pyuria affect the IDSA definition of asymptomatic bacteriuria?
o: It does not change it; the definition applies irrespective of pyuria
Pyuria converts the finding into a urinary tract infection
Pyuria lowers the threshold to 10³ CFU/mL
Pyuria must be absent for the definition to apply
renal-micro:culture.e: Pyuria alone does not make asymptomatic bacteriuria into symptomatic infection.

renal-micro:culture.q: A patient with a newly inserted catheter grows 10³ CFU/mL of one organism and has no symptoms. How is this read?
o: A contaminated specimen that should be discarded
True bacteriuria of unevaluated significance here
Sterile urine, since the count is below 10⁵
renal-micro:culture.e: IDSA accepts 10² to under 10⁵ from in-and-out or newly placed catheters as real bacteriuria.

renal-micro:culture.q: Why does Murray discourage urine screening tests such as dipstick chemistry and sediment stains?
o: They need a calibrated loop to interpret
They are insensitive for low-grade bacteriuria
They cross-react with protein in the urine
They cannot be done on refrigerated specimens
renal-micro:culture.e: Small numbers of organisms in a patient with pyuria can still matter clinically.

renal-micro:id.q: A urinary isolate is a gram-negative rod that grows on MacConkey agar and is oxidase negative. The next branch of the scheme is:
renal-micro:id.e: Oxidase negative plus glucose fermentation places it in Enterobacterales; lactose splits the family.

renal-micro:id.q: Colourless colonies on MacConkey that swarm on blood agar should be worked up with:
renal-micro:id.e: A swarming lactose non-fermenter from urine is usually Proteus mirabilis.

renal-micro:id.q: A positive PYR test can come from which two groups?
renal-micro:id.e: PYR must be read alongside other reactions; bile esculin and 6.5% NaCl confirm Enterococcus.

renal-micro:ast.q: In broth dilution testing, the MIC is:
o: The concentration that kills 99.9% of the inoculum
The drug level measured in the patient's serum
The lowest drug concentration that inhibits growth
The highest concentration the organism tolerates
renal-micro:ast.e: Dilutions are inoculated with a standardised suspension and read after overnight incubation.

renal-micro:ast.q: What does a larger zone of inhibition around a disk indicate?
o: The drug diffused poorly through the agar
The organism is more susceptible to that drug
renal-micro:ast.e: Under standardised conditions, zone diameter corresponds to the MIC.

renal-micro:ast.q: An isolate is reported intermediate, and the infection is confined to the bladder. Why can treatment still succeed?
o: Some drugs reach far higher concentrations in urine than in serum
Intermediate isolates always revert to susceptible in vivo
The bladder wall is impermeable to bacteria
Intermediate means the test was invalid
renal-micro:ast.e: Murray notes high urinary concentrations can eliminate organisms reported resistant; CLSI defines I partly by drugs that concentrate physiologically.

renal-micro:ast.q: How does the EUCAST category I differ from the CLSI category I?
o: EUCAST I is used only for urinary isolates
EUCAST I means susceptible at increased exposure
EUCAST I and CLSI I are defined identically
EUCAST I means the isolate is resistant at any dose
renal-micro:ast.e: The two systems are not interchangeable; the report must be read against the scheme the laboratory uses.

renal-micro:resist.q: ESBLs arose from which parent enzymes?
renal-micro:resist.e: Point mutations widened their spectrum to all penicillins and cephalosporins.

renal-micro:resist.q: Why do ESBLs spread so readily between organisms?
o: They are encoded on the bacterial chromosome only
They are packaged in bacterial spores
They are transmitted by bacteriophage lysis alone
renal-micro:resist.e: ESBLs are widespread in E. coli, Klebsiella and Proteus; E. coli and K. pneumoniae most often.

renal-micro:resist.q: Which mechanism explains vancomycin resistance in Enterococcus?
o: An efflux pump exports the drug
renal-micro:resist.e: Vancomycin normally binds the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus; a D-Ala-D-Lac terminus does not bind it. vanA and vanB can sit on plasmids.

renal-micro:resist.q: Which antibiotic class are enterococci naturally resistant to?
renal-micro:resist.e: That is why broad cephalosporin use selects for enterococcal UTI in long-stay patients.

renal-micro:other.q: Which virus establishes persistent latent infection of the kidney and causes disease in immunocompromised patients?
renal-micro:other.e: It reaches the kidney by viraemia in childhood and is otherwise benign.

renal-micro:other.q: Haemorrhagic cystitis in a child or an immunocompromised patient is associated with which adenovirus types?
renal-micro:other.e: Types 34 and 35 are also listed for haemorrhagic cystitis; 40 and 41 cause gastroenteritis.

renal-micro:other.q: How is Schistosoma haematobium infection diagnosed?
o: Eggs with a terminal spine in urine
Eggs with a lateral spine in stool
renal-micro:other.e: S. mansoni eggs carry a prominent lateral spine instead; disease comes from the immune response to eggs.

renal-clinical:hx.q: A patient voids small amounts many times a day. This is best described as:
renal-clinical:hx.e: Polyuria means a genuinely increased total daily volume.

renal-clinical:hx.q: Which single question best separates frequency from polyuria?
o: Whether it burns when you go
How often you go at night
How much comes out each time
renal-clinical:hx.e: Small volumes point to frequency, large volumes to polyuria.

renal-clinical:hx.q: A man reports difficulty starting his stream and a weak flow. This points to:
renal-clinical:hx.e: Hesitancy and a poor stream are storage-independent symptoms of outflow resistance.

renal-clinical:pain.q: Acute overdistention of the bladder characteristically causes:
renal-clinical:pain.e: Chronic distention, by contrast, is usually painless.

renal-clinical:pain.q: Pain from a stone passing down the ureter typically:
o: Comes in waves and radiates to the groin
Is steady and relieved by lying still
renal-clinical:pain.e: Patients are classically restless rather than still.

renal-clinical:pain.q: A patient with chronic urinary retention may have more than a litre in the bladder yet no complaint of pain. The clinical implication is that you must:
o: Reassure the patient it is harmless
Examine for it rather than rely on symptoms
renal-clinical:pain.e: Chronic distention is painless, so percussion and palpation are what detect it.

renal-clinical:incont.q: Leakage on coughing or sneezing is which type of incontinence?
renal-clinical:incont.e: Raised abdominal pressure overcomes poor urethral resistance.

renal-clinical:incont.q: Continuous dribbling from a bladder that never empties describes:
renal-clinical:incont.e: Neurologic disorders or obstruction prevent emptying until the bladder overdistends.

renal-clinical:incont.q: An alert patient with severe arthritis who cannot reach the toilet in time has which type of incontinence?
renal-clinical:incont.e: The urinary tract itself works normally; the limitation lies outside it.

renal-clinical:exam.q: The costovertebral angle is formed by the vertebrae and the:
renal-clinical:exam.e: It marks where kidney tenderness is elicited.

renal-clinical:exam.q: Why must the abdomen be auscultated before palpation?
renal-clinical:exam.e: The order differs from every other system for this reason.

renal-clinical:exam.q: Percussion of the costovertebral angle is performed when you suspect:
o: Infection or inflammation of the kidney
renal-clinical:exam.e: It is left to the end of the examination because it may be painful.

renal-clinical:record.q: Recording 'No costovertebral angle tenderness' is valuable because it tells the next reader:
o: The patient denied having any flank pain
Imaging of the kidneys is not required
The examination was done and was negative
renal-clinical:record.e: Otherwise they cannot tell a negative finding from an omitted one.

renal-clinical:record.q: A good physical examination record should contain:
renal-clinical:record.e: Interpretation belongs in the assessment, not the findings.

renal-clinical:record.q: Noting a past episode of pyelonephritis treated with ampicillin in the past medical history matters mainly because it:
o: Shapes the current differential and drug choice
Rules out an underlying structural anomaly
Confirms the diagnosis being considered now
Replaces the need for a urinalysis
renal-clinical:record.e: Previous infections and the drugs used, including any reaction to them, alter both what you suspect now and what you can safely prescribe.

renal-lab:spec.q: Urine left at room temperature for several hours before analysis typically shows:
o: A falling pH as bacteria multiply
An unchanged pH and intact casts
A rising pH as bacteria multiply
renal-lab:spec.e: Casts and cells also break down, so the sediment reads falsely low.

renal-lab:spec.q: A 24-hour urine collection is started by:
o: Timing from the first void onward
Discarding the first void then timing
Saving the first void then timing
renal-lab:spec.e: The final void at the 24-hour mark is included.

renal-lab:spec.q: A patient's measured creatinine clearance is unexpectedly low while serum creatinine is normal. Before diagnosing kidney disease, you should check that:
renal-lab:spec.e: An incomplete collection is the commonest source of error, and total daily creatinine output is used to verify it.

renal-lab:phys.q: The specific gravity pad on a urine dipstick measures:
renal-lab:phys.e: It may therefore disagree with a refractometer.

renal-lab:phys.q: One advantage of the dipstick method for specific gravity is that it is:
renal-lab:phys.e: Radiopaque contrast gives erroneous readings with a refractometer or urinometer.

renal-lab:phys.q: A patient whose urine specific gravity stays near 1.010 on every sample has:
o: Been drinking water to excess all day
Lost both concentrating and diluting ability
renal-lab:phys.e: Urine fixed at the specific gravity of plasma means the kidney can neither concentrate nor dilute it.

renal-lab:dip1.q: The urine dipstick ketone pad reacts with:
renal-lab:dip1.e: It does not react with acetone or beta-hydroxybutyrate.
It makes up more than three-quarters of the total, with acetoacetate about 10 percent.

renal-lab:dip1.q: A patient in severe diabetic ketoacidosis has only trace urine ketones that rise during treatment. This is because the dipstick:
o: Detects urinary ketones only above 50 mg/dL
Was read well before the reaction had developed
Misses beta-hydroxybutyrate, which converts back later
Is inhibited by the very high glucose concentration
renal-lab:dip1.e: The dominant ketone in severe acidosis is invisible to the pad until it is reoxidised to acetoacetate as the patient improves.

renal-lab:dip2.q: A urine dipstick shows a negative nitrite result although bacteria are seen microscopically. The likeliest reason is that the organism:
o: Produces urease and raised the pH
Was a contaminant from the skin
renal-lab:dip2.e: Not all uropathogens carry nitrate reductase.

renal-lab:dip2.q: Which cells do NOT contain the esterase detected by the leukocyte esterase pad?
renal-lab:dip2.e: Erythrocytes, bacteria and renal tubular cells lack it too, which limits the test's specificity.

renal-lab:dip2.q: Which finding would cause a false positive leukocyte esterase result?
renal-lab:dip2.e: High concentrations of some antibiotics, including tetracycline, cause false negatives instead.

renal-lab:sed.q: Finding a red blood cell cast localises bleeding to the:
renal-lab:sed.e: Casts can only form within tubules, so their contents must be renal.

renal-lab:sed.q: A sediment shows muddy brown granular casts. Which cast would instead have pointed to interstitial inflammation?
renal-lab:sed.e: Granular casts of this appearance belong to acute tubular injury.

renal-lab:sed.q: Oval fat bodies in the sediment indicate:
renal-lab:sed.e: They are lipid-laden tubular cells, and show a Maltese cross pattern under polarised light.

renal-lab:cryst.q: Which urinary crystal is abnormal whenever it is seen, so it always calls for further investigation?
renal-lab:cryst.e: The other three occur in normal urine depending on pH and concentration.

renal-lab:cryst.q: Triple phosphate (struvite) crystals form in urine that is:
renal-lab:cryst.e: Urease-producing organisms such as Proteus raise the pH.

renal-lab:cryst.q: A drowsy patient with a high anion gap acidosis has abundant envelope and dumbbell shaped crystals in the urine. The likely poisoning is:
renal-lab:cryst.e: It is metabolised to oxalate, which precipitates with calcium in the tubules.

renal-lab:prot.q: The urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio is useful because dividing by creatinine:
renal-lab:prot.e: A random sample can then substitute for a timed collection.

renal-lab:prot.q: A myeloma patient excretes large amounts of protein but the dipstick protein pad is negative. This is because the pad:
renal-lab:prot.e: Bence Jones protein needs electrophoresis with immunofixation.

renal-lab:prot.q: A healthy teenager has proteinuria on a daytime sample but none on a first morning sample. The likely explanation is:
renal-lab:prot.e: Protein appears only when upright and resolves on recumbency, and it is benign.

renal-lab:gfr.q: Creatinine clearance overestimates true GFR because creatinine is:
renal-lab:gfr.e: Filtration alone would give an accurate figure.

renal-lab:gfr.q: An elderly patient with little muscle mass has a normal serum creatinine. This may still conceal:
renal-lab:gfr.e: Creatinine production depends on muscle mass.

renal-lab:gfr.q: Why does early kidney disease often escape detection by serum creatinine?
o: The relationship with GFR is not linear
Creatinine is cleared by the liver too
Creatinine rises only in tubular disease
renal-lab:gfr.e: The first half of GFR can be lost with barely any rise in the measured value.

renal-lab:biomark.q: Cystatin C is a better marker of GFR than creatinine partly because it is:
renal-lab:biomark.e: Diet, age, sex and nutritional status also leave it unaffected.

renal-lab:biomark.q: At what clearance rate does cystatin C become abnormal?
renal-lab:biomark.e: This makes it more sensitive than creatinine.

renal-lab:biomark.q: KIM-1 is a useful marker of tubular injury because it is:
renal-lab:biomark.e: It is also absent from extrarenal tissue, so a rise points specifically at proximal tubular damage.

pharm-renal:oab.q: Mirabegron relieves overactive bladder by acting as a:
pharm-renal:oab.e: It relaxes the detrusor during filling, so it avoids antimuscarinic side effects.

pharm-renal:oab.q: Oxybutynin is relatively selective for which receptor?
pharm-renal:oab.e: Blocking it reduces involuntary detrusor contraction.

pharm-renal:oab.q: An 82-year-old on oxybutynin for urge incontinence becomes confused and constipated. The best alternative is:
pharm-renal:oab.e: Every alternative listed except the first is another antimuscarinic and would repeat the same problem; a beta-3 agonist avoids it.

pharm-renal:utiabx.q: Nitrofurantoin must not be used for pyelonephritis because it:
pharm-renal:utiabx.e: It concentrates in urine, which suits cystitis but not infection of the kidney itself.

pharm-renal:utiabx.q: Which organisms are inherently resistant to nitrofurantoin?
pharm-renal:utiabx.e: This limits its use when those organisms are suspected.

pharm-renal:utiabx.q: Nitrofurantoin has regained importance for uncomplicated urinary infection chiefly because:
o: It is active against Pseudomonas species
It can be given as a single oral dose
Resistance to other oral agents has risen
pharm-renal:utiabx.e: Rising resistance to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and the fluoroquinolones in E. coli has made it an important alternative, and its own resistance emerges slowly.

title.th: เคสใหญ่: ฉี่สีโค้ก

boss.case: A 7-year-old boy is brought in with puffy eyes and dark, cola-colored urine. Three weeks ago he had crusted, honey-colored skin sores on his legs. BP is 138/90 mm Hg. Urinalysis shows hematuria and protein 1+.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.e: Nephritic syndrome 2–4 weeks after group A strep skin or throat infection. IgA nephropathy follows a URI within days.

qs.q: Which urine sediment finding best supports this?

o: High C3 with normal ASO titers
Low C3 and high ASO/anti-DNase B
qs.e: Immune complexes activate complement; anti-DNase B is more reliable after skin infection.

qs.q: Electron microscopy of a biopsy would show:
qs.e: Light microscopy: hypercellular glomeruli; IF: granular 'starry sky' IgG, IgM, C3.

qs.q: His hypertension and edema are mainly due to:
o: Na⁺ and water retention from ↓ GFR
qs.e: Nephritic syndrome reduces filtration → volume expansion. Edema in nephrotic syndrome is driven by hypoalbuminemia.

o: Recurrent gross hematuria with every URI
Rapid progression to ESRD in most children
qs.e: Children usually recover; adults more often develop RPGN or CKD.

title.th: เด็กหน้าบวมตอนเช้า

stem.th: เด็กชาย 5 ปี ตาบวมตอนตื่นนอนมา 1 สัปดาห์ ตอนนี้ขาบวมด้วย ไม่มีไข้ ความดันปกติ
stem.en: A 5-year-old boy has had puffy eyes on waking for a week, now with leg swelling. No fever, normal BP.

info.th: UA: protein 4+, ไม่มีเม็ดเลือดแดง · albumin 1.8 g/dL · cholesterol สูง
info.en: UA: protein 4+, no RBCs · albumin 1.8 g/dL · high cholesterol

steps.q: Which syndrome fits best?
steps.e: Heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema and hyperlipidemia without hematuria = nephrotic syndrome.

steps.q: Most likely cause in this age group:
steps.e: Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children.

info.th: ทำ renal biopsy: LM ปกติ
info.en: Renal biopsy: light microscopy is normal

steps.q: What does electron microscopy show?
steps.e: MCD: diffuse foot-process effacement of podocytes; LM and IF are normal.

steps.q: Which part of the filtration barrier is chiefly disrupted?
steps.e: Loss of the podocyte slit diaphragm/polyanion barrier lets albumin leak (selective proteinuria).

steps.q: First-line treatment:
steps.e: MCD responds well to corticosteroids.

title.th: ปวดเอวร้าวลงขาหนีบ

stem.th: ชาย 35 ปี ปวดเอวขวาบิดเป็นพักๆ ร้าวลงขาหนีบ กระสับกระส่าย คลื่นไส้
stem.en: A 35-year-old man has colicky right flank pain radiating to the groin, restless and nauseated.

steps.q: Best initial imaging:
steps.e: Non-contrast CT shows stone size, site and obstruction; ultrasound is preferred in pregnancy.

info.th: CT: นิ่ว 5 mm ค้างที่ท่อไตส่วนปลายสุด
info.en: CT: 5 mm stone at the distal end of the ureter

steps.q: The narrowest point where stones commonly lodge here is the:
steps.e: Three constrictions: PUJ, pelvic brim (iliac vessels), and the UVJ, the narrowest.

steps.q: Most common stone composition:
steps.e: Calcium oxalate stones are the most common type.

steps.q: Which drug reduces calcium excretion to prevent recurrence?
steps.e: Thiazides increase distal Ca²⁺ reabsorption; loop diuretics increase calcium loss.

title.th: ปัสสาวะน้อยหลังช็อก

stem.th: หญิง 68 ปี หลังผ่าตัดลำไส้มีภาวะช็อกจากติดเชื้อ 6 ชม. วันต่อมาปัสสาวะออกน้อย creatinine ขึ้นจาก 0.9 เป็น 3.1
stem.en: A 68-year-old woman had 6 hours of septic shock after bowel surgery. Next day she is oliguric; creatinine rose from 0.9 to 3.1.

info.th: UA: muddy brown granular casts · FeNa 3%
info.en: UA: muddy brown granular casts · FENa 3%

steps.q: Most likely diagnosis:
steps.e: Muddy brown casts and FENa > 2% indicate intrinsic tubular injury (ATN).

steps.q: Which segments are most vulnerable to ischemia?
o: Papillary collecting ducts and thin limbs in the inner medulla
Proximal straight tubule and TAL in the outer medulla
steps.e: The pars recta and TAL have high O₂ demand in a poorly perfused outer medulla.

info.en: K⁺ 6.8 mEq/L · ECG shows peaked T waves

steps.q: First step in management:
steps.e: Calcium stabilizes the myocardium first; then shift K⁺ (insulin/glucose) and remove it.

steps.q: The granular casts are made of a matrix protein secreted by the:
steps.e: Casts form on a Tamm-Horsfall (uromodulin) matrix secreted by the TAL.

title.th: ไข้สูงปวดเอว

stem.th: หญิง 24 ปี ไข้ 39.2°C หนาวสั่น ปวดเอวซ้าย เคาะเจ็บ มีปัสสาวะแสบขัดมา 3 วัน
stem.en: A 24-year-old woman has fever 39.2°C, rigors and left flank pain with CVA tenderness after 3 days of dysuria.

info.th: UA: WBC มาก มี WBC casts, nitrite +
info.en: UA: many WBCs, WBC casts, nitrite positive

steps.q: Which finding localizes infection to the kidney rather than the bladder?
steps.e: Casts form in tubules, so WBC casts indicate renal parenchymal involvement.

steps.q: Most likely route of infection:
steps.e: Most pyelonephritis is ascending; the short female urethra favors this.

info.th: ถ้าดูเนื้อไตใต้กล้อง
info.en: If the kidney were examined histologically

steps.q: Expected histology:
o: Neutrophils in collecting ducts and interstitium
steps.e: Acute pyelonephritis: neutrophils fill tubules (especially collecting ducts) and interstitium.

steps.q: Most common organism:
steps.e: Uropathogenic E. coli causes most community UTIs.

title.th: เบาหวานสิบห้าปี

stem.th: ชาย 55 ปี เบาหวานชนิดที่ 2 มา 15 ปี คุมไม่ดี ตรวจสุขภาพประจำปี
stem.en: A 55-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes for 15 years comes for a check-up.

steps.q: The earliest structural change in diabetic kidney disease is:
steps.e: GBM thickening and mesangial expansion come first; nodules appear later.

steps.q: These nodules are called:
steps.e: Nodular glomerulosclerosis = Kimmelstiel–Wilson lesions.

steps.q: Which drug slows progression by lowering intraglomerular pressure?
steps.e: ACE inhibitors/ARBs dilate the efferent arteriole, lowering glomerular pressure and proteinuria.

steps.q: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis in diabetes classically affects:
steps.e: Diabetes involves both arterioles; hypertension mainly the afferent.

title.th: ปัสสาวะแสบขัดในหญิงสาว

stem.th: หญิง 26 ปี ปัสสาวะแสบขัดและบ่อยมา 2 วัน ไม่มีไข้ ไม่ปวดบั้นเอว แพทย์สั่งเพาะเชื้อปัสสาวะ
stem.en: A 26-year-old woman has 2 days of dysuria and frequency, without fever or flank pain. A urine culture is requested.

steps.q: Best specimen for routine urine culture here:
o: Suprapubic aspirate for the most reliable result
In-and-out catheter specimen to avoid any contamination
The first portion of the stream, which is most concentrated
Midstream voided specimen after discarding the first portion
steps.e: The first portion carries urethral flora and is discarded. Catheterisation is not recommended for routine cultures because it can itself induce infection.

info.th: พยาบาลถามว่าจะเก็บปัสสาวะอย่างไร
info.en: The nurse asks how the specimen should be collected

steps.q: Why does this matter?
o: Urinary pH falls and inhibits growth on MacConkey agar
Uropathogens multiply in urine, so the colony count is falsely high
Bacteria die in urine, so the culture turns falsely negative
White cells lyse, so pyuria can no longer be assessed
steps.e: Urinary tract pathogens grow in urine at room temperature. If plating is delayed the specimen should be refrigerated or kept in a bacteriostatic preservative.

info.th: ส่งถึงห้องปฏิบัติการช้า 3 ชั่วโมง เก็บที่อุณหภูมิห้อง
info.en: The specimen reaches the laboratory 3 hours later, having been kept at room temperature

steps.q: Given her symptoms, this count is best described as:
o: Insignificant unless a second specimen is obtained
Supporting infection, since she has urinary symptoms
Asymptomatic bacteriuria by the IDSA definition
Contamination, because only one organism grew
steps.e: The IDSA 10⁵ CFU/mL criterion defines asymptomatic bacteriuria, which requires the absence of symptoms. In a symptomatic patient the count supports infection, and lower counts with pyuria can still matter.

info.th: เพาะเชื้อขึ้น 10⁵ CFU/mL เป็นเชื้อชนิดเดียว
info.en: Culture grows 10⁵ CFU/mL of a single organism

steps.q: The organism is most likely:
steps.e: Lactose fermentation with a positive indole test and motility fits E. coli. Klebsiella is mucoid and non-motile; Proteus is a lactose non-fermenter that swarms.

info.th: Colony แบนสีชมพูบน MacConkey · indole ⊕ · เคลื่อนที่ได้
info.en: Flat pink colonies on MacConkey agar; indole positive and motile

steps.q: ESBLs arose from which enzymes, and why do they spread?
o: AmpC cephalosporinases induced by ceftazidime exposure
TEM-1 and SHV-1 after point mutations; most are plasmid-encoded
Altered penicillin-binding proteins transferred by transposons
steps.e: Point mutations in the TEM-1 and SHV-1 penicillinases widened their spectrum to all penicillins and cephalosporins. Most ESBLs sit on plasmids, so they move between organisms; E. coli and K. pneumoniae are the commonest hosts.

info.th: รายงานความไว: ดื้อ ceftriaxone และ ceftazidime · มีการสร้าง ESBL
info.en: Susceptibility report: resistant to ceftriaxone and ceftazidime; an ESBL is detected

title.th: คาสายสวนแล้วปัสสาวะขุ่น
title.en: Cloudy urine in a catheterised patient

stem.th: ชาย 72 ปี อัมพาตครึ่งล่าง คาสายสวนปัสสาวะมา 6 สัปดาห์ ปัสสาวะขุ่นและมีกลิ่นฉุน
stem.en: A 72-year-old paraplegic man has had an indwelling urinary catheter for 6 weeks. His urine is cloudy with a pungent smell.

steps.q: Which tests confirm the identification?
o: Optochin, bacitracin and the CAMP test
Oxidase, growth at 42 °C and pigment production
steps.e: A swarming lactose non-fermenter from urine is usually Proteus mirabilis: urease positive, motile and indole negative.

info.th: เพาะเชื้อขึ้นเชื้อที่คืบเป็นวงบน blood agar · lactose ⊖
info.en: Culture grows an organism that swarms across the blood agar and does not ferment lactose

steps.q: How did the organism produce the stone?
o: It secretes oxalate, which crystallises with calcium
It damages tubules and releases cystine into urine
It acidifies the urine so uric acid crystallises
steps.e: Urea is split into CO₂ and ammonia; the resulting alkaline urine precipitates magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite) and calcium apatite, and is itself toxic to the uroepithelium.

info.th: ปัสสาวะเป็นด่าง pH 8.2 · ภาพถ่ายพบนิ่วขนาดใหญ่ในกรวยไต
info.en: Urine pH is 8.2 and imaging shows a large stone filling the renal pelvis

steps.q: The matching stone type and urinary pH are:
o: Uric acid stone in acid urine
steps.e: Struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) stones form in alkaline urine produced by urease-positive organisms and can grow into staghorn calculi.

steps.q: Why does this film make treatment difficult?
o: It neutralises the urinary concentration of the drug
Its polysaccharide web shields them from drugs
It turns the organism into a cell-wall-deficient form
It blocks urine flow so the drug never reaches the bladder
steps.e: Biofilm is produced once the population reaches a quorum; it protects the organisms from immune clearance and antibiotics, and can trigger adaptive resistance.

info.th: เปลี่ยนสายสวน พบคราบลื่นเคลือบผิวด้านใน
info.en: The catheter is changed and its inner surface is coated with a slippery film

clues: Puffy eyes for 2 days; impetigo on legs 3 weeks ago
Creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, C3 low, C4 normal, ASO/anti-DNase B high
dx.e: Nephritic 1–4 weeks after group A strep; low C3 that normalizes in ~8 weeks.

clues: Started 1 day after a sore throat; similar episode last year
dx.e: Synpharyngitic hematuria with normal complement.

clues: Rapidly worsening fatigue and decreased urine over 2 weeks
Creatinine 1.1 → 4.8 mg/dL in 10 days; complement normal
Biopsy: crescents with linear IgG along GBM
dx.e: Antibodies against α3 NC1 of type IV collagen; treat with plasmapheresis + steroid + cyclophosphamide.

clues: Chronic sinusitis for months, weight loss
dx.e: Type III RPGN; PR3-ANCA, upper + lower airway + kidney.

clues: Bilateral sensorineural hearing loss; anterior lenticonus
dx.e: X-linked COL4A5 in ~85%.

clues: 6-year-old with a rash on the buttocks and legs
Abdominal pain and knee pain after a cold
dx.e: IgA vasculitis; renal lesion identical to IgA nephropathy.

clues: 4-year-old boy with swollen eyes in the morning
Albumin 1.8 g/dL, cholesterol high, creatinine normal
LM normal; EM: diffuse foot process effacement
dx.e: >90% of children respond to steroids.

clues: Albumin 2.4 g/dL; poor response to 16 weeks of prednisone
Biopsy: segmental sclerosis and hyalinosis in some glomeruli
dx.e: Common adult nephrotic cause; APOL1 risk in African ancestry; steroid-resistant often.

clues: 52-year-old man with gradually worsening ankle edema
Now sudden left flank pain and hematuria
dx.e: Primary MN = anti-PLA2R; renal vein thrombosis is a classic complication.
Leading cause of ESKD; GBM thickening is the first change.

clues: Albumin 2.1 g/dL; kidneys normal-sized on US despite CKD
dx.e: AA amyloid from chronic inflammation.

clues: 24-year-old woman with joint pain and facial rash
Low C3 and C4, anti-dsDNA high
Biopsy: diffuse proliferative GN with wire loops
dx.e: Most common and severe lupus class; 'full house' IF.

clues: Injection drug use in the past
Hepatitis C positive, cryoglobulins, low C4
dx.e: HCV/cryoglobulinemia → immune-complex MPGN.
Ischemic/septic ATN: FENa >1%, isosmotic urine.

clues: Diarrhea for 4 days, poor intake; takes lisinopril
Improves within 48 h of IV fluids
dx.e: Most common AKI; reversible with perfusion.

clues: Started on a β-lactam 10 days ago for cellulitis
dx.e: Stop the drug; steroids if not improving.

clues: Collapsed in heat during the race
dx.e: Aggressive fluids; watch K⁺ and Ca²⁺.

clues: Dipstick protein trace but urine protein high (light chains)
Biopsy: fractured casts with giant cells
dx.e: Light chain + Tamm–Horsfall casts.

clues: Dysuria for 3 days, then flank pain
dx.e: Ascending infection; WBC casts localize to kidney.
Triad: frequency, suprapubic pain, dysuria.

clues: Father died of a brain hemorrhage at 50
US: multiple cysts in both kidneys and liver
dx.e: PKD1 ~85%; berry aneurysms; tolvaptan.

clues: Liver: congenital hepatic fibrosis; PKHD1 mutation
dx.e: Fibrocystin defect.

clues: 35-year-old man with sudden severe left flank pain
